questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A G-alpha-s subunit is locked in its GTP-bound form. Which change is expected?
questions.explanation: Active G-alpha-s stimulates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and PKA activity. Intrinsic GTPase activity normally terminates the signal.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A cytokine receptor lacks intrinsic kinase activity but activates receptor-associated kinases that phosphorylate dimerizing transcription factors. Identify the pathway.
questions.explanation: Cytokine receptors commonly use JAKs to phosphorylate STAT proteins. STAT dimers then enter the nucleus and directly regulate transcription.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A steroid hormone response starts slowly but persists longer than a membrane-receptor response. What explains this?
options: Opening of a ligand-gated membrane ion channel
Alteration of gene transcription by intracellular receptor
Sequestration and storage of ligand in endosomes
Rapid enzymatic hydrolysis of membrane phospholipids
questions.answer: Alteration of gene transcription by intracellular receptor
questions.explanation: Steroid hormones cross membranes and bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors. Dependence on RNA and protein synthesis delays onset but prolongs the effect.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A receptor tyrosine kinase activates a small GTPase through an adaptor protein. Which downstream sequence promotes proliferation?
questions.explanation: Many receptor tyrosine kinases recruit adaptors that activate RAS, then RAF and MAP kinases. The cascade induces growth-related transcription.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A tumor cell secretes a growth factor that acts back on the same cell to sustain proliferation. This is:
questions.explanation: Autocrine signaling targets the secreting cell and can support tumor autonomy. Paracrine signals act on neighbors, whereas endocrine signals travel systemically.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A glomerular disease disrupts the sheet-forming collagen network of the basement membrane. Which collagen type is affected?
questions.explanation: Type IV collagen forms sheet-like basement-membrane networks. Types I and III are fibrillar collagens of interstitial matrix.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Emphysema causes loss of pulmonary recoil despite preserved collagen bundles. Which ECM protein has been degraded?
questions.explanation: Elastin allows lung and large arteries to stretch and recoil. Collagen supplies tensile strength but cannot provide elastic recoil.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Fibroblasts migrate through a hydrated provisional wound matrix rich in a large, non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan. Identify it.
questions.explanation: Hyaluronan binds abundant water and forms a loose matrix that facilitates migration. Unlike most glycosaminoglycans, it is non-sulfated and not linked to a core protein.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A migrating cell binds the RGD sequence of fibronectin and links it to actin. Which receptor family is involved?
questions.explanation: Integrins connect ECM proteins to the cytoskeleton and transmit signals bidirectionally. Cadherins chiefly mediate calcium-dependent cell-cell adhesion.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A carcinoma crosses a basement membrane. Which pair names its major adhesive glycoprotein and structural collagen?
questions.explanation: Basement membranes consist chiefly of laminin and a type IV collagen network with associated proteoglycans. Fibronectin and fibrillar collagen dominate interstitial matrix.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A disease-associated variant lies 80 kb upstream of an intact gene and chromosome-conformation analysis shows that this region loops to the promoter. Which element is altered?
questions.explanation: Enhancers are noncoding regulatory elements that influence promoters over long distances through chromatin looping. The intact coding region and distant position argue against an exon mutation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A tumor-suppressor gene is structurally normal but silent; its promoter has dense CpG methylation and compact chromatin. Which treatment most directly reverses this state?
questions.explanation: Promoter DNA methylation favors transcriptionally inactive chromatin. DNA methyltransferase inhibition may restore expression; the other drugs do not specifically reverse epigenetic promoter silencing.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Loss of a regulatory RNA-binding site in the 3-prime untranslated region stabilizes an oncogene mRNA and increases its translation. Which molecule normally binds there?
questions.explanation: MicroRNAs guide silencing complexes to complementary sequences, commonly in the 3-prime UTR, causing translational repression or mRNA degradation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Aberrant recruitment of histone deacetylase to a differentiation gene in leukemia will cause which immediate change?
questions.explanation: Deacetylation restores positive charge to histone lysines, strengthening histone-DNA interaction and condensing chromatin. The gene becomes less accessible to transcription machinery.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A guide RNA directs Cas9 to a mutant allele, and a supplied normal DNA template is copied into the break. Which repair pathway produced precise correction?
questions.explanation: Homology-directed repair uses a donor template for precise sequence replacement. Nonhomologous end joining is error-prone and more often introduces small insertions or deletions.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: After partial hepatectomy, a mesenchymal-cell ligand promotes hepatocyte survival, motility, and proliferation through MET. Identify it.
questions.explanation: Hepatocyte growth factor binds MET and is central to hepatocyte regeneration. PDGF primarily recruits mesenchymal cells, while VEGF targets endothelium.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A healing wound contains proliferating fibroblasts and smooth-muscle cells with recruited monocytes. Which platelet mediator best explains this?
questions.explanation: PDGF is chemotactic and mitogenic for fibroblasts and smooth-muscle cells and recruits monocytes, making it important in granulation tissue.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1-alpha in a carcinoma, inducing endothelial proliferation and vascular permeability. Which factor mediates this?
questions.explanation: VEGF is induced by hypoxia and is a dominant mediator of angiogenesis and vascular permeability. HGF acts mainly through MET on epithelial cells.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Rhizomelic limb shortening results from activation of a receptor that restrains growth-plate chondrocytes. Which receptor is mutated?
questions.explanation: Activating FGFR3 mutations inhibit endochondral growth and cause achondroplasia. It is a gain-of-function defect despite reduced skeletal growth.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Chronic inflammation progresses to fibrosis. Which mediator increases collagen synthesis while suppressing matrix degradation?
questions.explanation: TGF-beta is the principal fibrogenic cytokine, activating fibroblasts, increasing ECM synthesis, and decreasing matrix breakdown.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A child has coarse facies, skeletal abnormalities, and high plasma levels of lysosomal hydrolases. The enzymes are synthesized normally but fail to enter lysosomes. Which Golgi modification is defective?
questions.explanation: Mannose-6-phosphate directs lysosomal hydrolases from the trans-Golgi to lysosomes. Without this tag, the enzymes follow the constitutive secretory pathway and appear in plasma.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: An LDL receptor binds LDL normally but cannot cluster in coated pits. Which process is specifically impaired?
questions.explanation: LDL-receptor complexes concentrate in clathrin-coated pits before entering endosomes. Normal ligand binding cannot compensate for defective coated-pit internalization.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A drug inhibits the 26S proteasome. Which material accumulates most directly?
questions.explanation: Proteasomes recognize and degrade polyubiquitinated cytosolic and nuclear proteins. Bacteria and whole organelles require lysosomal degradation or autophagy.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A renal tubular epithelial cell loses separation of apical and basolateral membrane domains. Which function is most affected?
questions.explanation: Epithelial polarity places different transporters on opposite surfaces, enabling directional absorption and secretion. Loss of polarity mixes these systems and disrupts vectorial transport.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A toxin prevents microtubule polymerization. Which event fails first?
questions.explanation: Microtubules are tracks for kinesin and dynein and also form the mitotic spindle. Actin and intermediate filaments perform the other listed cytoskeletal functions.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A newborn generates heat in brown fat by oxidizing substrate without a proportional increase in ATP. Which protein is responsible?
questions.explanation: UCP-1 permits proton re-entry into the matrix without ATP synthase, dissipating the gradient as heat. This is nonshivering thermogenesis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: A tumor converts glucose to lactate despite adequate oxygen. What is the main growth advantage?
options: Maximum ATP yield per glucose molecule
questions.explanation: The Warburg effect sacrifices ATP efficiency while preserving carbon intermediates for macromolecular synthesis. Oxidative phosphorylation would burn more substrate completely to carbon dioxide and water.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: After DNA damage, BAX and BAK oligomerize in the outer mitochondrial membrane. Which event commits the cell to intrinsic apoptosis?
options: Mitochondrial swelling with rapid ATP loss
Cytochrome c release and apoptosome formation
questions.answer: Cytochrome c release and apoptosome formation
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization releases cytochrome c, stabilizing the apoptosome and activating caspases. Permeability transition is more closely linked to ATP failure and necrosis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: An affected woman transmits a mitochondrial DNA disorder to all children, but an affected man transmits it to none. Why?
options: Mitochondrial genes lie on X chromosome
The ovum supplies nearly all zygotic mitochondria
All mitochondrial proteins are maternally encoded
questions.answer: The ovum supplies nearly all zygotic mitochondria
questions.explanation: The fertilized ovum receives almost all cytoplasmic organelles from the mother, producing maternal inheritance of mtDNA. Most mitochondrial proteins are nevertheless nuclear encoded.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Ischemia opens mitochondrial permeability transition pores and dissipates the proton gradient. Which immediate consequence follows?
options: Increased complex V ATP synthesis activity
Oxidative phosphorylation failure and ATP depletion
Cyclin D dependent kinase complex activation
questions.answer: Oxidative phosphorylation failure and ATP depletion
questions.explanation: The inner-membrane proton gradient powers ATP synthase. Its collapse halts oxidative phosphorylation and contributes to ion-pump failure and necrotic injury.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: DNA damage stabilizes p53 and arrests a cell before S phase. Which p53 target directly inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes?
questions.explanation: p53 induces p21, producing G1/S arrest and time for repair. Irreparable damage can instead lead to senescence or apoptosis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Mitogenic signaling raises cyclin D-CDK4 activity. Which event permits passage through the G1 restriction point?
questions.explanation: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB, releasing E2F to induce S-phase genes. Hypophosphorylated RB restrains E2F.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Which normally quiescent population can proliferate substantially after tissue loss?
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes are stable cells that reside in G0 but re-enter the cycle after injury or partial hepatectomy. Neurons and cardiac myocytes are permanent cells.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: One stem-cell daughter retains stemness while the other becomes a committed progenitor. This pattern is called:
questions.explanation: Asymmetric division preserves the stem-cell pool while generating differentiating progeny. Signals from the stem-cell niche influence this balance.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.chapterTitle: The Cell as a Unit of Health and Disease
questions.prompt: Fibroblasts receive OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and MYC and acquire the ability to form derivatives of all three germ layers. They are:
questions.explanation: These transcription factors can reprogram somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells. Their broad differentiation potential is balanced by concerns about genomic instability and tumor formation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A malformation is best defined as:
options: A primary intrinsic error of morphogenesis
Secondary destruction of a previously normal structure
Fetal compression by abnormal mechanical forces
A localized overgrowth of mature native tissue
questions.answer: A primary intrinsic error of morphogenesis
questions.explanation: Malformations reflect an intrinsically abnormal developmental process.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A breech fetus in a small uterus develops clubfeet and hip dislocation without intrinsic abnormality of limb patterning. The abnormality reflects compression during growth rather than abnormal organogenesis. Which category fits?
questions.explanation: Deformations arise from mechanical constraint acting on the developing fetus.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A disruption is caused by:
options: Primary genetic error occurring during organogenesis
Secondary breakdown of previously normal developing tissue
Postnatal malignant tumor embolization to tissues
questions.answer: Secondary breakdown of previously normal developing tissue
questions.explanation: Disruptions arise from extrinsic injury to tissue that began development normally.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A deformation results from:
options: Clonal neoplastic proliferation of embryonal cells
Extrinsic mechanical forces altering fetal form
Excess surfactant accumulation in terminal saccules
questions.answer: Extrinsic mechanical forces altering fetal form
questions.explanation: Deformations are caused by biomechanical forces such as uterine constraint.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Amniotic bands are a classic cause of:
questions.explanation: Amniotic bands can encircle and destroy previously normal fetal parts.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Uterine constraint is a common cause of:
questions.explanation: Constraint compresses the fetus and alters shape or position.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A sequence means:

Cascade of anomalies initiated by one primary defect
Benign mesenchymal hamartoma composed of mature tissue
Malignant embryonal blastema presenting at birth

questions.explanation: A sequence is a chain reaction from a single initiating abnormality.

questions.prompt: A syndrome is:

Recognized pattern of anomalies with a common cause
Elevated oncofetal serum biomarker in maternal serum

questions.prompt: Atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysms classically occur:
questions.explanation: AAAs usually occur in the infrarenal abdominal aorta.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Aortic dissection begins when blood enters the media through:
questions.explanation: An intimal tear permits blood to dissect through the media.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The most important risk factor for aortic dissection in older adults is:
questions.explanation: Hypertension is the major risk factor for dissection.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Marfan syndrome predisposes to aortic dissection because of:
options: Medial degeneration with elastic tissue fragmentation
Unprovoked deep venous thrombosis with embolization
questions.answer: Medial degeneration with elastic tissue fragmentation
questions.explanation: Connective tissue weakness causes medial degeneration and wall fragility.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old smoker has a 6.2-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with mural thrombus. The media is thinned beneath severe atherosclerosis. What is the most feared acute complication?
questions.explanation: Large AAAs can rupture into the retroperitoneum or peritoneal cavity.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A hypertensive man suddenly develops tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Blood tracks through the aortic media, creating a false channel for several centimeters. Which event initiated the lesion?
options: Intimal tear with medial dissection by blood
Rupture of descending venous valve leaflets
questions.answer: Intimal tear with medial dissection by blood
questions.explanation: Aortic dissection is blood dissecting through the media after intimal disruption.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Atherosclerosis primarily affects which vessels?
questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis is an intimal disease of elastic and muscular arteries.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: After aortic catheterization, a patient develops blue toes and renal dysfunction. Biopsy of a small artery shows elongated empty clefts surrounded by inflammation. Which atherosclerotic complication is most likely?
questions.explanation: Disrupted plaques can release cholesterol crystals that leave needle-shaped clefts in tissue.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The earliest visible lesion of atherosclerosis is the:
questions.explanation: Fatty streaks are intimal collections of lipid-laden foam cells.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Which lipoprotein is most directly implicated in atheroma formation?
questions.explanation: LDL enters the intima, becomes modified, and drives foam cell formation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Foam cells in atherosclerotic lesions are mainly:
options: Macrophages and smooth muscle cells with ingested lipid
Megakaryocytes with alpha and dense core granules
Tissue mast cells displaying surface bound IgE
questions.answer: Macrophages and smooth muscle cells with ingested lipid
questions.explanation: Macrophages and smooth muscle cells can accumulate lipid and become foam cells.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Oxidized LDL promotes atherogenesis because it is:
options: Cleared exclusively by native regulated LDL receptors
Proinflammatory and taken up by scavenger receptors
Inhibits monocyte recruitment across the endothelium
Directly digests collagen in the fibrous cap
questions.answer: Proinflammatory and taken up by scavenger receptors
questions.explanation: Modified LDL stimulates inflammation and is ingested by macrophage scavenger receptors.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Which plaque is least likely to rupture?
options: Plaque with thin inflamed fibrous cap and necrosis
Plaque with dense macrophage infiltration at shoulder
Plaque with thick fibrous cap and small lipid core
Plaque with large necrotic lipid core and hemorrhage
questions.answer: Plaque with thick fibrous cap and small lipid core
questions.explanation: Thick collagen-rich caps are more stable than thin inflamed caps.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The major modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis include:
options: Advancing age, male sex, and family history
ABO erythrocyte blood group antigen profile
Adult height and constitutional hair pigmentation
questions.explanation: These factors injure endothelium or alter lipid and inflammatory responses.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A man dies suddenly from coronary thrombosis. Autopsy shows a plaque with a large necrotic core, many macrophages at the shoulder, and a very thin fibrous cap that has ruptured. Which feature made this plaque vulnerable?
options: Thin inflamed fibrous cap over a large lipid core
Dense medial calcification without luminal narrowing
A pure fatty streak without necrosis
questions.answer: Thin inflamed fibrous cap over a large lipid core
questions.explanation: Vulnerable plaques have thin caps, lipid-rich cores, and abundant inflammation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A macrophage in the arterial intima keeps taking up modified LDL despite becoming cholesterol-rich. The responsible uptake pathway is not down-regulated by intracellular cholesterol. Which receptor class explains this?
questions.explanation: Scavenger receptors internalize modified LDL without normal feedback suppression.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Benign hypertension classically causes:
questions.explanation: Chronic hypertension causes plasma protein leakage and smooth muscle wall thickening.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A hypertensive patient dies of hemorrhage in the basal ganglia. Autopsy reveals rupture of tiny aneurysmal dilations in penetrating arteries rather than a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis. Which lesion is implicated?
questions.explanation: Long-standing hypertension can produce microaneurysms in small penetrating cerebral vessels.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Malignant hypertension classically causes:
questions.explanation: Severe hypertension produces onion-skin arteriolar thickening.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are associated with:
questions.explanation: Hypertension weakens small penetrating brain arteries.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis in diabetes is promoted by:
options: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in perivascular space
Direct fungal hyphal invasion through the vessel media
Endothelial injury with plasma protein leakage into walls
Reed-Sternberg cell infiltration along internal elastic lamina
questions.answer: Endothelial injury with plasma protein leakage into walls
questions.explanation: Diabetes and hypertension both cause homogeneous hyaline arteriolar thickening.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The microscopic 'onion-skin' lesion of malignant hypertension is due to:
options: Accumulation of subendothelial foam cell fatty streaks
Ectatic cavernous vascular channels with organized thrombi
Concentric smooth muscle proliferation and membrane duplication
questions.answer: Concentric smooth muscle proliferation and membrane duplication
questions.explanation: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis has laminated concentric arteriolar thickening.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Fibrinoid necrosis in malignant hypertension reflects:
options: Arteriolar wall injury with plasma protein deposition
Benign dystrophic medial calcification without necrosis
Passive venous congestion with ectatic vascular channels
Perivascular AL amyloid light chain fibril deposition
questions.answer: Arteriolar wall injury with plasma protein deposition
questions.explanation: Severe pressure damages endothelium and vessel walls.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The kidney in benign nephrosclerosis typically shows:
questions.explanation: Chronic arteriolar narrowing causes ischemic renal scarring.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A patient with BP 245/145 mm Hg develops headache, renal failure, papilledema, and retinal hemorrhages. Renal arterioles show onion-skin lesions with areas of fibrinoid necrosis. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Malignant hypertension causes acute vascular injury with hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis and necrotizing arteriolitis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A long-standing diabetic patient has renal arterioles with homogeneous eosinophilic wall thickening and luminal narrowing. Similar lesions are common in chronic hypertension. Which lesion is present?
questions.explanation: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is seen in diabetes and benign hypertension.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Giant cell arteritis most often occurs in:
questions.explanation: Giant cell arteritis is typically a disease of patients older than 50 years.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: An elderly patient with suspected temporal arteritis is started on high-dose corticosteroids before biopsy results return. What complication is this urgent treatment intended to prevent?
questions.explanation: Visual loss from arterial occlusion can be sudden and permanent in giant cell arteritis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Takayasu arteritis is classically associated with:
options: Painless temporal headache in elderly only
questions.explanation: Takayasu arteritis can narrow aortic arch branches, causing pulseless disease.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The vessel commonly biopsied in suspected giant cell arteritis is the:
questions.explanation: Temporal artery biopsy may show granulomatous inflammation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Giant cell arteritis can cause sudden blindness by involving the:
questions.explanation: Ocular ischemia is a feared complication requiring urgent therapy.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Both giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis are characterized by:
options: IgA immune complex deposition in venules
questions.explanation: Both are granulomatous large-vessel vasculitides.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Takayasu arteritis most commonly involves the:
options: Aortic arch and great vessel branches
questions.answer: Aortic arch and great vessel branches
questions.explanation: Aortic arch branch stenosis explains pulse deficits and blood pressure differences.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Jaw claudication in giant cell arteritis reflects:
options: Extensive thrombosis of pterygoid venous plexus
Ischemia of mastication muscles from inflamed arteries
questions.answer: Ischemia of mastication muscles from inflamed arteries
questions.explanation: Cranial arterial narrowing can cause pain while chewing.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A 72-year-old has new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, high ESR, and visual blurring. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Giant cell arteritis affects older adults and branches of carotid arteries.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old woman has diminished radial pulses, arm claudication, ocular symptoms, and different blood pressures in the two arms. Imaging shows narrowing of aortic arch branches. Which vasculitis best fits?
questions.explanation: Takayasu arteritis is granulomatous inflammation of the aorta and major branches in younger patients.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Polyarteritis nodosa primarily affects:
questions.explanation: PAN is a necrotizing arteritis of medium-sized arteries.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A young heavy smoker has severe pain in fingers and toes, superficial nodular phlebitis, and segmental thrombosing inflammation containing microabscesses in small and medium arteries. Symptoms improve only with smoking cessation. Which disease is present?
questions.explanation: Buerger disease is a smoking-associated thrombosing vasculitis of extremity vessels.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Kawasaki disease is most important because it can cause:
questions.explanation: Kawasaki disease can damage coronary arteries in children.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Thromboangiitis obliterans is strongly linked to:
questions.explanation: Buerger disease occurs in smokers and affects extremity vessels.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Classic polyarteritis nodosa characteristically spares the:
questions.explanation: PAN often involves renal, visceral, and coronary arteries but not pulmonary arteries.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Polyarteritis nodosa has been associated with infection by:
questions.explanation: Some PAN cases are linked to immune complexes containing HBV antigens.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The acute mucocutaneous syndrome with fever, conjunctivitis, oral erythema, rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy in a child suggests:
questions.explanation: Kawasaki disease is also called mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Thromboangiitis obliterans typically affects:
questions.explanation: Buerger disease causes segmental thrombosing inflammation of extremity vessels.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A middle-aged patient has fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, hypertension, renal infarcts, and aneurysmal nodularity in renal and mesenteric arteries. Lung vessels are spared. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: PAN is a necrotizing medium-vessel vasculitis with renal/visceral involvement and pulmonary sparing.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A 3-year-old child has persistent fever, conjunctival injection, strawberry tongue, erythema of palms and soles, desquamation, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Weeks later, echocardiography detects coronary aneurysms. Which disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: Kawasaki disease affects children and can produce coronary arteritis with aneurysms.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: Raynaud phenomenon is caused by episodic vasospasm of:
questions.explanation: Raynaud causes color changes in fingers or toes after cold or stress.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: An elderly patient has pipe-stem calcification of muscular arteries on radiograph, but distal pulses are preserved and the lumen is not significantly narrowed. Which vascular change is present?
questions.explanation: Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis calcifies the media but usually does not obstruct flow.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: Primary Raynaud phenomenon is also called:
questions.explanation: Primary Raynaud occurs without an associated disease.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: Fibromuscular dysplasia most often affects:
questions.explanation: Renal artery involvement may cause secondary hypertension.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: Secondary Raynaud phenomenon can be associated with:
questions.explanation: Connective tissue diseases can cause structural vascular disease with Raynaud symptoms.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: The angiographic pattern classically associated with fibromuscular dysplasia is:
questions.explanation: Alternating stenosis and dilation creates a beaded appearance.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: Medial calcific sclerosis is characterized by:
options: Transmural necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of wall
Medial calcification without significant luminal narrowing
Prominent mesangial IgA immune complex deposition
questions.answer: Medial calcification without significant luminal narrowing
questions.explanation: Monckeberg sclerosis is often an incidental radiologic finding.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: Fibromuscular dysplasia is best described as:
options: Atherosclerotic lipid plaque with fibrous cap rupture
Bacterial endarteritis with mycotic wall destruction
questions.explanation: FMD is a noninflammatory stenosing disease of medium-sized arteries.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: A young woman has severe hypertension. Renal angiography shows alternating stenotic and dilated segments of the renal artery, but there is no lipid plaque, vasculitis, or thrombus. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: FMD causes renal artery stenosis in young women and has a string-of-beads appearance.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Raynaud Phenomenon, Fibromuscular Dysplasia, and Other Noninflammatory Disorders
questions.prompt: A patient’s fingers turn white, then blue, then red after cold exposure. Nailfold capillaries are normal and no autoimmune disease is found. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Primary Raynaud is functional vasospasm without an associated structural disease.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is classically associated with:
questions.explanation: PR3-ANCA/c-ANCA is strongly associated with GPA.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A child develops palpable purpura on the legs, colicky abdominal pain, arthralgia, and hematuria after an upper respiratory infection. Vessel walls and glomeruli show IgA deposition. Which mechanism is central?
options: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture with cholesterol emboli
questions.explanation: IgA vasculitis is an immune complex small-vessel vasculitis involving skin, gut, joints, and kidneys.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Microscopic polyangiitis is commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: MPO-ANCA/p-ANCA is common in microscopic polyangiitis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: IgA vasculitis was formerly called:
questions.explanation: IgA vasculitis causes purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal disease.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis commonly involves:
questions.explanation: GPA causes necrotizing granulomas and small-vessel vasculitis in these sites.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Microscopic polyangiitis differs from polyarteritis nodosa because it:
options: Characteristically spares kidneys and urinary system completely
Confined strictly to ascending thoracic aorta and its branches
Produces aneurysmal dilation of epicardial coronary vessels
Involves microvasculature and causes necrotizing glomerulonephritis
questions.answer: Involves microvasculature and causes necrotizing glomerulonephritis
questions.explanation: MPA is a small-vessel vasculitis and may cause pulmonary capillaritis and GN.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is strongly associated with:
questions.explanation: EGPA features asthma, eosinophilia, and necrotizing vasculitis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis refers to:
options: Clonal lymphoid malignancy invading postcapillary walls
Neutrophilic small-vessel inflammation with nuclear debris
Smooth muscle hamartomatous proliferation around arterioles
Dystrophic calcification confined strictly to arterial media
questions.answer: Neutrophilic small-vessel inflammation with nuclear debris
questions.explanation: Fragmented neutrophils create leukocytoclasia in small vessel walls.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A patient has chronic sinusitis, otitis media, cavitary lung nodules, hematuria, and crescentic glomerulonephritis. Biopsy shows necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis. Which antibody is most expected?
questions.explanation: GPA is associated with PR3-ANCA and necrotizing granulomatous respiratory disease.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A patient develops pulmonary hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Biopsy shows necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis without granulomas or immune deposits. MPO-ANCA is positive. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: MPA is a pauci-immune ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis without granulomatous inflammation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The most common benign tumor of infancy is:
questions.explanation: Infantile hemangiomas are common benign vascular tumors.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A worker exposed to vinyl chloride develops a hemorrhagic malignant liver tumor composed of atypical endothelial cells forming irregular vascular channels. Which tumor is most likely?
questions.explanation: Vinyl chloride, arsenic, and thorotrast exposure are linked to hepatic angiosarcoma.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Pyogenic granuloma is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: Despite its name, pyogenic granuloma is a capillary proliferation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor of:
questions.explanation: Angiosarcoma is an aggressive endothelial malignancy.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of:
questions.explanation: Cavernous hemangiomas have large blood-filled spaces.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Kaposi sarcoma is associated with infection by:
questions.explanation: Human herpesvirus 8 is required for Kaposi sarcoma.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Bacillary angiomatosis is caused by:
questions.explanation: Bartonella causes vascular proliferations, especially in immunocompromised patients.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Lymphangiomas are best considered:
questions.explanation: Lymphangiomas are developmental lymphatic lesions, often in children.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: An AIDS patient develops multiple violaceous skin plaques. Biopsy shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, extravasated red cells, and hemosiderin. Which viral association is required for this tumor?
questions.explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-associated vascular neoplasm.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A pregnant patient develops a rapidly growing, red, pedunculated gingival lesion that bleeds easily. Histology shows lobular proliferation of capillaries in an edematous stroma. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pyogenic granuloma is a reactive lobular capillary hemangioma and may occur during pregnancy.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: Which vascular layer is directly exposed to flowing blood and normally provides an antithrombotic surface?
questions.explanation: The intima contains endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: Tertiary syphilis damages the small vessels that nourish the thoracic aortic wall. The aortic media becomes ischemic and scarred, predisposing to ascending aortic dilation. Which structure is primarily injured?
questions.explanation: Obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum causes medial ischemia and thoracic aneurysm.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: Which endothelial products normally promote vasodilation and inhibit platelet activation?
questions.explanation: NO and prostacyclin maintain flow by relaxing smooth muscle and limiting platelet activation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: The principal contractile cells of the tunica media are:
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle cells regulate vascular tone and respond to injury.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: During acute inflammation, endothelial activation is important because it:
options: Inhibits all downstream inflammatory cytokine signaling
Eliminates platelet binding to extracellular matrix components
Transforms muscular arteries into capacitance venules
Increases leukocyte adhesion and procoagulant activity
questions.answer: Increases leukocyte adhesion and procoagulant activity
questions.explanation: Activated endothelium expresses adhesion molecules and favors leukocyte recruitment and thrombosis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: Restenosis after angioplasty is mainly driven by:
options: Smooth muscle migration, proliferation, and matrix synthesis
Monocyte apoptosis and lipid core expansion
questions.answer: Smooth muscle migration, proliferation, and matrix synthesis
questions.explanation: Vascular injury stimulates intimal smooth muscle proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: Vasa vasorum are most important in large vessels because they:
options: Supply the avascular intima and inner media
Supply the outer media and adventitia
Anchor vascular smooth muscle to basal lamina
questions.answer: Supply the outer media and adventitia
questions.explanation: Large vessels are too thick to be nourished entirely by diffusion from the lumen.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: Loss of endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability favors which combination of changes?
questions.explanation: Endothelial dysfunction promotes abnormal tone, thrombosis, and inflammatory recruitment.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: A diabetic smoker has coronary arteries with impaired vasodilation, increased endothelial adhesion molecule expression, and platelet activation before severe luminal narrowing is present. Which early abnormality best links these risk factors to later plaque formation?
questions.explanation: Atherosclerotic risk factors dysregulate endothelium, enabling lipid entry, inflammation, and thrombosis-prone behavior.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Vascular Wall, Endothelial Cells, and Smooth Muscle Cells
questions.prompt: Months after balloon angioplasty, a coronary segment narrows again. Histology shows intimal smooth muscle proliferation with abundant extracellular matrix but no necrotizing vasculitis. Which process explains this restenosis?
questions.explanation: Restenosis is a repair response caused by smooth muscle migration/proliferation and matrix deposition.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Varicose veins result primarily from:
options: Venous valve incompetence and chronic dilation
Deep venous thrombosis with recanalization failure
Lymphatic hypoplasia with interstitial fluid stasis
questions.answer: Venous valve incompetence and chronic dilation
questions.explanation: Valve failure causes venous pooling and dilation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: After axillary lymph node dissection and radiation therapy for breast cancer, a patient’s arm becomes chronically swollen with thickened skin and recurrent infections. Which process explains the swelling?
options: Chronic venous insufficiency from deep reflux
Complex regional pain syndrome type I
questions.explanation: Surgery and radiation can obstruct lymphatic drainage and produce chronic lymphedema.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Deep venous thrombosis is clinically important mainly because it can lead to:
questions.explanation: Leg DVT can embolize to pulmonary arteries.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Lymphedema is edema caused by impaired:
questions.explanation: Lymphatic obstruction causes protein-rich interstitial fluid accumulation.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Esophageal varices most often develop because of:
questions.explanation: Portal hypertension diverts blood through portosystemic collaterals.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Migratory thrombophlebitis is also known as:
questions.explanation: Trousseau syndrome may accompany visceral malignancy.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Chronic venous insufficiency can cause:
questions.explanation: Sustained venous hypertension injures skin and subcutaneous tissues.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Elephantiasis is most often caused worldwide by:
questions.explanation: Filarial infection can obstruct lymphatics and cause massive lymphedema.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A cirrhotic patient vomits large amounts of blood. Endoscopy shows dilated tortuous submucosal veins at the gastroesophageal junction. Which hemodynamic abnormality produced these vessels?
options: Portal hypertension with portosystemic collateral formation
Hepatic vein outflow obstruction without collateral flow
Superior mesenteric artery thrombosis with ischemia
questions.answer: Portal hypertension with portosystemic collateral formation
questions.explanation: Esophageal varices form when portal pressure is diverted to systemic venous channels.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma develops recurrent tender superficial venous thromboses that appear in different sites over several months. Which vascular complication is this?
questions.explanation: Mucin-producing cancers can cause a hypercoagulable state with Trousseau syndrome.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by:
options: Biventricular hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction
Myocardial fibrosis with isolated diastolic dysfunction
questions.explanation: DCM has impaired contractility and dilated chambers.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A patient with plasma cell dyscrasia develops heart failure with normal-sized ventricles, biatrial enlargement, thick stiff walls, and Congo red-positive deposits. Which mechanism best explains the physiology?
questions.explanation: Amyloid deposition causes a stiff, poorly filling restrictive heart.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy commonly involves mutation in genes encoding:
questions.explanation: HCM is often caused by mutations in contractile apparatus proteins.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Restrictive cardiomyopathy primarily causes:
questions.explanation: Stiff ventricles restrict diastolic filling.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The classic histology of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is:
options: Diffuse interstitial fibrosis with wavy myocytes
questions.explanation: Myofiber disarray is a characteristic microscopic feature of HCM.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A common infiltrative cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy is:
questions.explanation: Amyloid deposition stiffens the ventricular walls.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Viral myocarditis is most commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: Viral myocarditis shows lymphocytes with myocyte necrosis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Chagas myocarditis is caused by:
questions.explanation: T. cruzi can cause chronic myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A young athlete dies suddenly during exertion. The heart has asymmetric septal hypertrophy, small LV cavity, and histologic myofiber disarray. Which disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: HCM causes asymmetric hypertrophy and is an important cause of sudden death in young athletes.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A patient with alcohol use disorder develops four-chamber dilation, mural thrombi, and reduced ejection fraction. Histology shows nonspecific myocyte hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis. Which cardiomyopathy pattern is present?
questions.explanation: Toxic injury such as alcohol can produce DCM with systolic failure.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: The most common congenital cardiac anomaly is:
questions.explanation: VSD is the most common congenital heart defect.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A neonate has severe cyanosis soon after birth. The aorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, creating two parallel circulations. Which additional feature is necessary for survival?
options: Complete closure of the ductus arteriosus
A communication allowing mixing of blood
questions.answer: A communication allowing mixing of blood
questions.explanation: Transposition requires a shunt such as ASD, VSD, or PDA to permit mixing.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Left-to-right shunts initially cause:
questions.explanation: Oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Tetralogy of Fallot includes:
options: ASD, pulmonary atresia, left ventricular hypoplasia, and dextrocardia
Truncus arteriosus, single ventricle, aortic atresia, and mitral cleft
Endocardial cushion defect, coarctation, bicuspid valve, and LV dilation
VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy
questions.answer: VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy
questions.explanation: These four features define tetralogy of Fallot.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Eisenmenger syndrome means:
options: Reversal of a left-to-right shunt due to pulmonary hypertension
Sudden enlargement of an atrial septal defect with embolization
Persistent right-to-left shunt without vascular remodeling
Obliteration of the ductus arteriosus causing right heart failure
questions.answer: Reversal of a left-to-right shunt due to pulmonary hypertension
questions.explanation: Long-standing increased pulmonary flow can cause irreversible pulmonary vascular disease and cyanosis.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Patent ductus arteriosus connects the:
questions.explanation: The ductus arteriosus normally links pulmonary artery and aorta in fetal life.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Coarctation of the aorta in adults is classically associated with:
options: Upper extremity hypotension and bounding femoral pulses
Continuous machinery murmur and wide systemic pulse pressure
Upper extremity hypertension and weak femoral pulses
Cyanosis localized strictly to the upper extremities
questions.answer: Upper extremity hypertension and weak femoral pulses
questions.explanation: Postductal coarctation causes high arm pressure and low leg pressure.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Transposition of the great arteries requires survival through:
options: A mixing lesion such as VSD, ASD, or PDA
questions.answer: A mixing lesion such as VSD, ASD, or PDA
questions.explanation: Parallel circuits are incompatible with life unless blood mixes.
questions.subject: Pathology

Isolated arterial hypoperfusion with cerebral syncope
Severe orthopnea, paroxysmal dyspnea, and pulmonary crackles

Centrilobular congestion alternating with paler periportal zones
Portal tract expansion with bridging fibrosis and piecemeal necrosis
Nodular regenerative hyperplasia with central vein obliteration

Pulmonary hypertension from lung or pulmonary vascular disease
Severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with elevated left atrial pressure

Fixed coronary stenosis limiting flow during increased demand
Coronary artery dissection with acute intramural hematoma

questions.prompt: Prinzmetal angina is caused primarily by:

Gradual luminal narrowing from stable plaque
Coronary vasospasm in normal epicardial vessels

questions.explanation: Unstable angina is part of acute coronary syndrome and often follows plaque rupture.

questions.prompt: Silent myocardial ischemia is especially common in patients with:
questions.explanation: Autonomic neuropathy in diabetes can blunt ischemic pain.

Valvular vegetation detachment with septic embolization

Early transmural fibrinous pericarditis on day two

Sudden syncope caused by complete atrioventricular block
Recurrent episodes of Prinzmetal variant vasospasm

questions.topic: Atelectasis, Pulmonary Edema, and Acute Lung Injury
questions.prompt: Atelectasis means:

Permanent dilation of bronchi from inflammation
Destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis
Diffuse alveolar infiltration with proteinaceous fluid

questions.topic: Atelectasis, Pulmonary Edema, and Acute Lung Injury
questions.prompt: A patient with acute myocardial infarction develops dyspnea and pink frothy sputum. Lungs are heavy and wet, and alveoli contain transudate with heart failure cells. Which mechanism caused the edema?

questions.topic: Atelectasis, Pulmonary Edema, and Acute Lung Injury
questions.prompt: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema most often results from:

questions.topic: Atelectasis, Pulmonary Edema, and Acute Lung Injury
questions.prompt: Diffuse alveolar damage is the histologic pattern of:
questions.explanation: ARDS is characterized by diffuse alveolar damage.

questions.topic: Atelectasis, Pulmonary Edema, and Acute Lung Injury
questions.prompt: Resorption atelectasis commonly occurs when:

Loss of pulmonary surfactant increases alveolar surface tension
Fibrotic retraction prevents full expansion of the pulmonary lobe
An airway obstruction prevents air entry distal to the blockage

questions.prompt: Compression atelectasis can be caused by:

Fibrin-rich edema fluid and necrotic epithelial debris
Extracellular amyloid fibrils derived from serum proteins
Precipitated mucin droplets and eosinophil granules

questions.topic: Atelectasis, Pulmonary Edema, and Acute Lung Injury
questions.prompt: Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema in ARDS is caused by:

questions.topic: Atelectasis, Pulmonary Edema, and Acute Lung Injury

questions.subject: Pathology

questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Charcot-Leyden crystals are derived from:

questions.prompt: The classic inflammatory cell in allergic asthma is:

questions.topic: Asthma, Cystic Fibrosis, and Small Airway Disease
questions.prompt: Airway remodeling in asthma includes:
options: Alveolar septal destruction and airspace enlargement
Extensive plexiform arteriolar lesions and medial hypertrophy
Smooth muscle hypertrophy and basement membrane thickening
Subpleural honeycombing with dense fibroblastic foci

questions.explanation: Chronic asthma causes structural thickening of airway walls.

questions.prompt: The most common lethal pulmonary complication of cystic fibrosis is:

questions.prompt: Bronchiolitis obliterans refers to:
options: Fibrotic narrowing or obliteration of small airways
Acute diffuse alveolar collapse from lack of surfactant
Malignant squamous transformation of bronchial mucosa

questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Asthma, Cystic Fibrosis, and Small Airway Disease

questions.prompt: Restrictive lung disease is characterized by reduced:

questions.prompt: A farmer develops dyspnea, cough, and fever hours after handling moldy hay. Biopsy shows interstitial pneumonitis with poorly formed granulomas after repeated antigen exposure. Which disorder is likely?

questions.prompt: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis shows the histologic pattern called:

questions.prompt: Sarcoidosis is characterized by:

questions.prompt: Temporal heterogeneity is a feature of:

questions.prompt: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is caused by:
options: Immune reaction to inhaled organic antigens
Inhalation of inert crystalline silica dust
Inhalation of mineral amphibole asbestos fibers

questions.subject: Pathology

Pleural mesothelial cells and vascular elastica

questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: A young adult has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, skin nodules, uveitis, and lung biopsy with tight noncaseating granulomas but no organisms. Which systemic disease best fits?

questions.explanation: Airflow obstruction is most evident during expiration.

questions.subject: Pathology

Permanent enlargement of airspaces with wall destruction
Fibrotic obliteration of terminal and respiratory bronchioles

questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Obstructive Lung Disease: Emphysema, Chronic Bronchitis, Asthma, Bronchiectasis
questions.prompt: Chronic bronchitis is clinically defined by persistent productive cough for:
options: At least 2 weeks in two consecutive years
At least 6 months during a single year
At least 1 month during seasonal winter shifts
At least 3 months in 2 consecutive years
questions.answer: At least 3 months in 2 consecutive years
questions.explanation: The definition is based on chronic productive cough after excluding other causes.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.topic: Obstructive Lung Disease: Emphysema, Chronic Bronchitis, Asthma, Bronchiectasis
questions.prompt: Centriacinar emphysema is most strongly associated with:

questions.prompt: Asthma is driven by:

Nonreversible fibrotic remodeling of distal bronchioles
Primary necrotizing infection of cartilaginous bronchi

questions.prompt: Bronchiectasis is best defined as:

Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles without fibrosis
Acute purulent consolidation of an entire pulmonary lobe by pyogenic bacteria
Permanent dilation of bronchi due to chronic necrotizing infection or obstruction

questions.subject: Pathology

To suppress circulating leukocyte production globally

questions.explanation: Inflammation removes microbes or damaged tissue and sets the stage for tissue repair.

Chronic autoimmune reaction characterized by lymphoid follicles
Transient vasoconstriction followed by fibrotic replacement
Rapid onset with fluid exudation and neutrophilic infiltrate

questions.explanation: Acute inflammation begins quickly, is usually short-lived, and commonly features edema and neutrophils.

Rapidly progressive liquefaction driven by neutrophils
Short-lived vascular leakage resolving without scarring
Transient histamine release from perivascular mast cells
questions.answer: Prolonged duration with mononuclear infiltration and fibrosis
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation combines continuing injury, macrophages/lymphocytes, tissue damage, and attempts at healing.

options: Clear serous fluid with few scattered lymphocytes
Abundant thick fibrin strands without cellular elements
Epithelioid granulomas with multinucleated giant cells
Pus rich in neutrophils and liquefactive debris

questions.explanation: Suppurative inflammation contains neutrophils, necrotic debris, and edema fluid.

A sterile transudate in a serous cavity

questions.explanation: Abscesses are focal suppurative lesions with central liquefactive necrosis and many neutrophils.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: An ulcer is:
options: A walled-off collection of suppurative liquefactive exudate
A local surface defect from sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue
A circumscribed focus of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells
A diffuse non-demarcated spreading interstitial phlegmon

questions.prompt: Complete resolution of acute inflammation is most likely when:
options: Extensive stromal framework destruction has occurred
Infectious organisms persist continuously in the focus
Injury is limited, short-lived, and tissue can regenerate
Abundant fibrin fails to clear from serosal surfaces
questions.answer: Injury is limited, short-lived, and tissue can regenerate
questions.explanation: Resolution requires removal of mediators/debris and preservation of regenerative capacity and tissue framework.

questions.prompt: Organization and scarring are favored when:
options: The basement membrane scaffold remains fully intact
Neutrophils undergo rapid clearance without parenchymal necrosis
Mediators dissipate rapidly with preservation of architecture
There is substantial tissue destruction or abundant fibrinous exudate

questions.explanation: If exudate or necrotic tissue cannot be cleared, granulation tissue grows into it and collagen scar forms.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: Progression from acute to chronic inflammation is most likely when:

Neutrophils undergo prompt apoptosis and macrophages clear debris
The basement membrane is intact and injury is trivial
questions.answer: The injurious agent persists or normal healing is interfered with
questions.explanation: Persistent infection, foreign material, autoimmune injury, or delayed clearance can convert acute inflammation into chronic inflammation.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: A fibrinous pericarditis can either resolve or become organized. Organization means:
options: Rapid enzymatic clearance of fibrin by native plasminogen
Fibroblast and vascular ingrowth resulting in fibrous union
Transformation of exudative fluid into serous effusion
Spontaneous restoration of original mesothelial lining

questions.explanation: Organization is replacement of fibrinous exudate by granulation tissue and eventually fibrous scar.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Tissue repair occurs by which two broad processes?
questions.explanation: Repair restores tissue by regenerating cells and/or forming scar through connective tissue deposition.

questions.prompt: During scar maturation, early type III collagen is gradually replaced mainly by:
questions.explanation: Healing scars become stronger as type I collagen replaces the initially deposited type III collagen.

questions.prompt: Labile cells are cells that:
questions.explanation: Labile tissues, such as epithelia and hematopoietic cells, have continuous cell turnover.
questions.subject: Pathology

questions.prompt: Permanent cells are best exemplified by:
options: Vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts
questions.explanation: Permanent cells have little or no proliferative ability, so injury usually heals by scar.
