questions.explanation: During the ATLS primary survey resuscitation phase, after managing Airway, Breathing, and Circulation, the three standard screening radiographs for an unconscious or severely injured polytrauma patient are: 1. Cervical spine lateral (or rapid pan-scan CT); 2. Chest anteroposterior (AP); and 3. Pelvis AP (to rapidly identify life-threatening hemorrhage from pelvic ring disruption). Individual extremity radiographs are performed during the secondary survey.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: In standard orthopaedic radiography, what are the components of the clinical 'Rule of Twos'?
options: Two views, two joints, two limbs in children, and two occasions
Two observers, two radiological modalities, two contrast agents, and two exposures
Two planes, two orthogonal cuts, two millimeters slice thickness, and two repeats
Two projections, two energy levels, two digital detectors, and two limb positions
questions.answer: Two views, two joints, two limbs in children, and two occasions
questions.explanation: The 'Rule of Twos' in orthopaedic radiology consists of: 1. Two views: Anteroposterior (AP) and lateral, as a fracture visible in one projection may be completely concealed in the other; 2. Two joints: Must include the joint above and joint below the fractured bone; 3. Two limbs: In pediatric patients with open growth plates, compare with the uninjured opposite limb; 4. Two occasions: Repeat radiograph immediately after reduction, and after 1-2 weeks if an undisplaced or stress fracture is suspected.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child presents with elbow pain and swelling following a fall from monkey bars. Why is a comparative radiograph of the contralateral uninjured elbow essential before ruling out a fracture?
options: Unossified cartilaginous centers can simulate or conceal fractures
Excessive cortical thickness prevents penetration of diagnostic X-ray beams
Severe osteopenia in normal children eliminates bony anatomical contrast
Absence of periosteal sleeve in immature bone leads to invisible displacements
questions.answer: Unossified cartilaginous centers can simulate or conceal fractures
questions.explanation: The pediatric elbow has six secondary ossification centers that appear and fuse at predictable ages (CRITOE: Capitulum 1y, Radial head 3y, Internal/medial epicondyle 5y, Trochlea 7y, Olecranon 9y, External/lateral epicondyle 11y). Non-ossified cartilage is radiolucent, and normal physeal lines can be misdiagnosed as fractures, or displaced avulsion fragments misdiagnosed as normal centers. A comparative film of the normal elbow prevents catastrophic errors.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: In orthopaedic clinical practice, after what time interval is an untreated or neglected fracture formally classified as an 'old fracture'?
questions.explanation: According to standard orthopaedic definitions, an untreated fracture presenting more than 3 weeks after trauma is categorized as an 'old fracture'. By 3 weeks, early soft callus and fibrous tissue have organized between the fragments, making simple closed reduction impossible without formal open mobilization, osteoclasis, or osteotomy.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old male with an open distal femoral fracture presents with an expanding pulsatile hematoma in the popliteal fossa, absent distal pedal pulses, and a cold, pale foot. What is the immediate management requirement?
options: Immediate surgical exploration without delaying for angiography
Formal CT angiography in radiology suite followed by elective vascular review
Application of skeletal traction and Doppler ultrasound observation for 6 hours
Immediate closed reduction under hematoma block with observation in recovery
questions.answer: Immediate surgical exploration without delaying for angiography
questions.explanation: 'Hard signs' of arterial injury include: 1. Active, pulsatile arterial bleeding; 2. Expanding or pulsatile hematoma; 3. Palpable thrill or audible bruit; 4. Absent distal pulses; 5. Obvious signs of distal limb ischemia (pale, cold, mottled, pulseless extremity). The presence of hard signs mandates immediate emergency surgical exploration and vascular repair without wasting precious warm ischemia time on non-invasive imaging.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male with a closed midshaft tibial fracture in an above-knee cast develops excruciating leg pain 8 hours post-injury. The pain is refractory to IV morphine and is exacerbated by passive extension of the toes. The anterolateral compartment is tense and woody. Distal pedal pulses are palpable. What is the immediate management step?
options: Bivalve cast, split padding to skin, and prepare for fasciotomy
Elevate limb above heart level and administer high-dose intravenous mannitol
Inject local lidocaine into anterior compartment and apply cold ice compression
Perform immediate closed reduction and apply a tighter unpadded plaster cast
questions.answer: Bivalve cast, split padding to skin, and prepare for fasciotomy
questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion to injury and pain elicited by passive stretching of compartment muscles are the earliest and most reliable signs of acute compartment syndrome. The presence of palpable peripheral pulses does NOT rule out compartment syndrome (pulses disappear only in late/terminal stages). The immediate intervention is to remove all constricting dressings (split cast and padding down to skin) and prepare for emergent surgical fasciotomy.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: When assessing compartment syndrome using needle manometry, what delta-P threshold (diastolic blood pressure minus intracompartmental pressure) mandates emergency surgical fasciotomy?
options: Delta P of 30 mmHg or less
Delta P of 50 mmHg or less
Delta P of 70 mmHg or less
Delta P of 15 mmHg or less
questions.answer: Delta P of 30 mmHg or less
questions.explanation: Tissue perfusion is determined by the pressure gradient between microvascular perfusion pressure and tissue pressure. An absolute compartment pressure > 30-40 mmHg or, more accurately, a delta-P (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) of 30 mmHg or less indicates critical tissue ischemia and mandates emergency decompression by fasciotomy.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male sustains closed bilateral femoral fractures. Thirty-six hours after admission, he develops acute confusion, tachypnea (respiratory rate 34/min), PaO2 of 54 mmHg on room air, and petechial hemorrhages across the anterior chest and conjunctivae. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fat Embolism Syndrome typically presents 24 to 72 hours following closed long-bone (especially femur) or pelvic fractures. Gurd's diagnostic criteria require at least one major sign and four minor signs, or two major signs. Major signs include: 1. Respiratory insufficiency (tachypnea, PaO2 < 60 mmHg); 2. Neurological depression/confusion; 3. Subconjunctival and axillary/chest petechial rash (pathognomonic, caused by fat emboli occluding dermal capillaries).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental biological distinction between delayed union and non-union of a fracture?
options: Reparative osteogenesis remains active in delayed union, ceased in non-union
Delayed union requires bone grafting, non-union heals with simple cast rest
Delayed union exhibits eburnated sclerotic bone, non-union shows wide callus
Delayed union is irreversible, non-union spontaneously consolidates in 6 months
questions.answer: Reparative osteogenesis remains active in delayed union, ceased in non-union
questions.explanation: Delayed union means the fracture is taking longer than the expected average time to unite for that specific bone, but the fracture gap remains open, vascularity is preserved, and union can still be achieved with continued immobilization. Non-union implies that all reparative processes have ceased, the bone ends have become rounded and sclerotic (or atrophic/tapered), the medullary canal is sealed by bone, and a false joint (pseudoarthrosis) has formed.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male with an isolated midshaft tibial fracture presents 8 months post-injury with persistent pain on weight-bearing and demonstrable mobility. Radiographs show a persistent radiolucent gap flanked by flared, dense, sclerotic bone ends resembling an 'elephant's foot'. What is the diagnosis and surgical treatment principle?
options: Hypertrophic non-union; requires rigid mechanical stabilization without mandatory bone grafting
Atrophic non-union; requires massive autologous cancellous bone grafting with cast immobilization
Infected non-union; requires radical bone resection and long-term antibiotic beads
Oligotrophic non-union; requires low-intensity pulsed ultrasound without internal fixation
questions.answer: Hypertrophic non-union; requires rigid mechanical stabilization without mandatory bone grafting
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic non-union (vascular/elephant-foot) occurs when biological healing potential and blood supply are excellent, but mechanical stability is inadequate (excessive interfragmentary motion). Abundant fibrocartilage forms, producing flared sclerotic ends. Treatment focuses strictly on restoring rigid mechanical stability (e.g., reamed interlocking intramedullary nailing); bone grafting is generally unnecessary.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old female presents 9 months after an open, severely stripped forearm fracture with painless abnormal mobility. Radiographs show pencil-thin, tapered, osteopenic bone ends separated by a wide radiolucent gap with no visible callus. What is the fundamental surgical requirement for this atrophic non-union?
options: Excision of fibrous tissue, opening canals, bone grafting, and rigid plating
Prolonged functional cast bracing with low-intensity pulsed ultrasound
Closed intramedullary nailing without opening non-union site or grafting
Isolated dynamic compression plating alone without cancellous grafting
questions.answer: Excision of fibrous tissue, opening canals, bone grafting, and rigid plating
questions.explanation: Atrophic non-union is characterized by a complete failure of biological osteogenesis and poor vascularity. The bone ends are tapered, rounded, and avascular ('pencil-in-cup' or 'horse's foot'). Treatment requires both biological stimulation (freshening bone ends, opening sclerosed medullary canals, decortication, and autologous cancellous bone grafting) and mechanical stability with rigid plate fixation.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old woman sustains a distal radius fracture treated in a tight cast for 6 weeks. Two weeks after cast removal, she presents with severe burning pain in the hand out of proportion to the original trauma, diffuse hand edema, hyperesthesia, warmth, and finger stiffness. Radiographs show patchy, spotty osteopenia ('ground-glass' osteoporosis). What is the diagnosis?
options: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I
questions.answer: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I
questions.explanation: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (CRPS I), historically known as Sudeck's atrophy or reflex sympathetic dystrophy, is an exaggerated neurovascular and autonomic response to trauma (often minor or following tight cast immobilization). It presents with burning pain, allodynia, hyperpathia, autonomic dysregulation (edema, color and temperature changes), and progressive joint stiffness. Radiographs classically reveal spotty, patchy juxta-articular osteoporosis.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 14-year-old boy sustains an elbow dislocation that is successfully reduced. His parents take him for vigorous daily massage and forced passive extension exercises. Three weeks later, the elbow is tender and stiff, and radiographs reveal a cloudy mass of new bone forming within the brachialis muscle anterior to the elbow joint. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Myositis ossificans, stop massage and stretching, splint and let mass mature
Immediate emergency surgical excision of the immature ectopic bone mass
Aggressive passive manipulative stretching under general anesthesia
High-dose systemic corticosteroid injections directly into the muscle mass
questions.answer: Myositis ossificans, stop massage and stretching, splint and let mass mature
questions.explanation: Myositis ossificans traumatica is heterotopic bone formation within muscle or periarticular soft tissues following trauma, classically occurring in the brachialis muscle after elbow injuries subjected to vigorous massage or forceful passive manipulation. Management requires immediate cessation of massage/passive stretching, resting the joint in a splint until the acute inflammatory phase subsides, followed by active gentle mobilization. Premature excision causes severe recurrence; excision is considered only after the mass has fully matured on radiograph (6-12 months).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What is the earliest and most sensitive imaging modality for detecting avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head following an intracapsular fracture, before plain radiographs show any changes?
options: Magnetic Resonance Imaging demonstrating a low-signal T1 band and 'double-line sign' on T2
High-resolution CT scan showing subchondral trabecular condensation
Contrast-enhanced ultrasound showing joint capsule thickening
Standing pelvic radiograph measuring the acetabular roof index
questions.answer: Magnetic Resonance Imaging demonstrating a low-signal T1 band and 'double-line sign' on T2
questions.explanation: MRI is the gold standard and most sensitive diagnostic tool for detecting early avascular necrosis (Ficat-Arlet Stage 0/I), detecting microvascular ischemia weeks to months before plain radiographs show osteopenia, sclerosis, or the 'crescent sign' of subchondral collapse. Classically, MRI demonstrates a serpentine band of low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and the pathognomonic 'double-line sign' on T2-weighted images.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: In established Volkmann's Ischaemic Contracture (VIC) of the forearm, what is the classic deformity of the wrist and fingers, and which muscle group is primarily fibrosed?
options: Wrist flexion, MCP hyperextension, and IP flexion from volar flexor fibrosis
Wrist extension, MCP flexion, and IP extension from extensor muscle fibrosis
Thumb adduction deformity alone caused by isolated adductor pollicis fibrosis
Ulnar claw hand attitude caused by isolated deep motor ulnar nerve transaction
questions.answer: Wrist flexion, MCP hyperextension, and IP flexion from volar flexor fibrosis
questions.explanation: Volkmann's Ischaemic Contracture is the end-stage cicatricial sequela of untreated compartment syndrome of the forearm. The deep flexor compartment—chiefly Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) and Flexor Pollicis Longus (FPL)—suffers ischemic infarction and turns into inelastic fibrous scar tissue. This produces the classic deformity: wrist flexion, MCP hyperextension, and severe IP flexion. A key sign is that finger extension can be increased only by simultaneously flexing the wrist (Volkmann's sign).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: What is the anatomical distinction between a joint dislocation and a subluxation?
options: Dislocation is complete loss of contact, subluxation is partial loss
Dislocation involves articular fracture, subluxation is purely ligamentous
Dislocation spontaneously reduces, subluxation requires open surgical repair
Dislocation preserves joint capsule, subluxation tears all periarticular tissues
questions.answer: Dislocation is complete loss of contact, subluxation is partial loss
questions.explanation: According to standard orthopaedic definitions, a dislocation (luxation) represents complete, total disruption of joint congruity such that the articulating bone surfaces lose all anatomical contact with each other. In a subluxation, there is partial displacement and incongruity, but a portion of the opposing articular cartilages remains in contact.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: Why is an acute dislocation of a major joint (such as the hip or knee) an orthopaedic emergency requiring immediate reduction?
options: Compresses adjacent vessels, risking avascular necrosis or ischemia
Triggers immediate systemic fat embolism and acute respiratory distress
Rapidly induces irreversible purulent septic arthritis within hours
Causes systemic rhabdomyolysis and life-threatening hyperkalemic arrest
questions.answer: Compresses adjacent vessels, risking avascular necrosis or ischemia
questions.explanation: Acute joint dislocation is an emergency because the displaced skeletal ends exert direct tension, compression, or kinking on vital periarticular neurovascular structures. For example, in hip dislocation, the retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head are stretched, risking avascular necrosis (the risk escalates dramatically if reduction is delayed > 6 hours); in knee dislocation, popliteal artery occlusion risks limb amputation.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: A 20-year-old collegiate gymnast sustains an acute posterolateral elbow dislocation. Following prompt, uncomplicated closed reduction under procedural sedation, what is the mandatory immediate clinical step?
options: Neurovascular assessment followed by post-reduction radiographs
Immediate application of a full circular rigid above-elbow plaster cast
Urgent computed tomography with three-dimensional vascular rendering
Forceful active range-of-motion testing to assess joint stability
questions.answer: Neurovascular assessment followed by post-reduction radiographs
questions.explanation: Immediately after reducing any dislocation, the surgeon must: 1. Re-evaluate and document neurovascular integrity (e.g., in elbow dislocation, assess radial pulse, capillary refill, and motor/sensory function of median, radial, and ulnar nerves); 2. Obtain orthogonal post-reduction radiographs to confirm concentric reduction and exclude previously obscured fractures; 3. Gently assess range of motion and joint stability to determine the safe arc of movement.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: In recurrent anterior dislocation of the shoulder, what pathological lesion consists of an avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum with the attached inferior glenohumeral ligament?
questions.explanation: A Bankart lesion is the primary essential lesion predisposing to recurrent anterior shoulder instability: it is an avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum from the glenoid rim, typically accompanied by disruption of the anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament complex (IGHLC). A Hill-Sachs lesion is a compression fracture of the posterolateral humeral head caused by impaction against the hard anterior glenoid rim.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: What clinical feature distinguishes recurrent dislocation of the patella from habitual dislocation of the patella in adolescents?
options: Recurrent is episodic, habitual occurs every time knee flexes
Recurrent occurs exclusively in boys, habitual occurs only in elderly females
Recurrent dislocates medially, habitual dislocates obligatorily laterally
Recurrent requires vastus medialis release, habitual heals with brace rest
questions.answer: Recurrent is episodic, habitual occurs every time knee flexes
questions.explanation: Recurrent patellar dislocation is episodic, often starting after an initial traumatic subluxation and recurring during pivoting or twisting movements in patients with underlying predisposing factors (e.g., high Q angle, patella alta, trochlear dysplasia). Habitual patellar dislocation occurs obligatorily and painlessly every time the knee flexes, almost always caused by an abnormal fibrous band or tight contracture of the vastus lateralis / iliotibial band tethering the patella laterally during flexion.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: An 8-year-old girl falls from a swing onto her outstretched hand. Radiographs of the distal radius reveal a fracture line passing across the growth plate and traversing vertically through the epiphysis into the articular joint space. According to the Salter-Harris classification, this is classified as:
questions.explanation: Salter-Harris Type III is an intra-articular physeal injury where the fracture runs along the physis and exits through the epiphysis into the joint. Type I is a pure transverse separation through the physis. Type II passes through the physis and exits through the metaphysis (creating a triangular Thurston-Holland sign). Type IV crosses through the metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis in continuity.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: Which Salter-Harris physeal injury pattern is statistically the most common, accounting for approximately 75% of all growth plate fractures?
questions.explanation: Salter-Harris Type II is by far the most frequent physeal fracture (~75%). The shear force cleaves the weak hypertrophic zone of the physis and directs obliquely into the metaphysis, producing a characteristic triangular metaphyseal fragment known as the Thurston-Holland sign. The periosteal hinge remains intact on the metaphyseal side, facilitating stable closed reduction.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 9-year-old boy sustains a displaced Salter-Harris Type IV fracture of the distal femoral physis. What surgical principle is essential to prevent progressive angular deformity, bone bridging (physeal bar), and leg-length discrepancy?
options: Anatomical reduction with smooth wires parallel to the physis
Closed reduction with multiple threaded screws crossing the growth plate
Long-leg unpadded circular cast immobilization without reduction
Immediate epiphysiodesis of the contralateral normal distal tibia
questions.answer: Anatomical reduction with smooth wires parallel to the physis
questions.explanation: Salter-Harris Type IV is an intra-articular fracture crossing metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis. If reduced with any step-off or gap, endochondral ossification forms an osseous bridge across the physis (physeal bar), resulting in asymmetric tethering, severe angular deformity, and limb shortening. Anatomic reduction and stabilization using smooth K-wires (or screws placed strictly within the epiphysis and metaphysis without traversing the physis) are mandatory.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: Why do incomplete greenstick fractures occur almost exclusively in growing children rather than in mature adult bone?
options: Thick vascular periosteum combined with elastic, porous, compliant cortical bone
Higher concentration of insoluble crystalline hydroxyapatite in pediatric bone
Continuous plastic deformation occurring under low torsional forces in adult bone
Complete absence of Haversian canals in immature pediatric skeletons
questions.answer: Thick vascular periosteum combined with elastic, porous, compliant cortical bone
questions.explanation: Greenstick fractures reflect the unique biomechanical properties of immature pediatric bone: the bone has high water and collagen content, lower mineral density, and greater elasticity. Under bending forces, the bone behaves like a green twig—the cortex on the convex (tension) side breaks while the cortex on the concave (compression) side buckles without complete fracture, held securely by a thick, tough periosteal sleeve.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: When evaluating the spontaneous remodeling potential of malunited pediatric long-bone fractures, which deformity has the LEAST capacity for spontaneous correction by skeletal growth?
options: Angular deformity in the plane of adjacent hinge joint movement
Metaphyseal angular deformity near an active growth plate
Appositional bayonet displacement with mild shortening in a child under 8 years
questions.explanation: Pediatric bone remodels based on the Heuter-Volkmann law and Wolff's law. Remodeling is greatest for: 1. Younger children with significant remaining growth; 2. Fractures near an active growth plate (metaphyseal); 3. Angular deformities in the plane of joint motion (flexion-extension). In contrast, rotational (torsional) deformities do NOT correct spontaneously with growth and persist into adult life unless surgically realigned.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 5-year-old girl sustains a closed midshaft femoral fracture. The surgeon deliberately accepts 1.0 to 1.5 cm of bayonet appositional shortening during closed reduction and spica casting. What physiological phenomenon justifies this decision?
options: Post-traumatic hyperemic overgrowth over the next 1 to 2 years
Premature physeal arrest causing permanent progressive limb shortening
Excessive muscle traction preventing anatomical end-to-end alignment
Spontaneous longitudinal remodeling that selectively shortens bone
questions.answer: Post-traumatic hyperemic overgrowth over the next 1 to 2 years
questions.explanation: In children aged 2 to 10 years, femoral fractures stimulate increased regional vascularity and hyperemia during fracture healing, accelerating physeal growth plates. This causes 1 to 2 cm of longitudinal overgrowth of the injured femur over the next 18 to 24 months. Therefore, an initial 1 cm of bayonet apposition and shortening is desirable to prevent long-term limb length inequality (overlengthening).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 7-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with unexplained swelling and irritability. Skeletal survey reveals multiple fractures at varying stages of healing, including metaphyseal bucket-handle avulsions and posterior rib fractures near the costovertebral junctions. What condition must be suspected?
questions.explanation: The radiological constellation of fractures of different healing ages, metaphyseal corner/bucket-handle fractures (caused by violent twisting or shaking), posterior rib fractures (caused by thoracic squeezing), and spinous process fractures is pathognomonic for non-accidental injury (battered baby syndrome / physical abuse). It demands immediate hospitalization, child protection notification, and a full multidisciplinary forensic evaluation.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What is the mechanical mechanism of a pediatric torus (buckle) fracture commonly seen in the distal radius?
options: Axial compression causing impaction and cortical wrinkling
Torsional stress causing spiral disruption of both cortical surfaces
Tensile distraction causing failure on the tension side of cortex
Direct lateral shear causing transverse displacement through physis
questions.answer: Axial compression causing impaction and cortical wrinkling
questions.explanation: A torus or buckle fracture is a classic pediatric compressive injury. Axial load (e.g., fall on an outstretched hand) compresses the porous, compliant trabecular bone of the distal radial metaphysis, producing acute buckling or bulging of the cortex. There is no true cortical disruption, no displacement, and it heals reliably within 3 weeks in a simple splint or cast.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old boy presents with a malunited supracondylar fracture of the humerus resulting in a severe gunstock deformity (cubitus varus). What is the primary anatomical component of the malunion responsible for this deformity?
options: Medial tilting and internal rotation of the distal fragment
Complete premature growth arrest of the lateral condylar physis
Avascular necrosis of the trochlea and capitulum
Lateral translocation of the olecranon process
questions.answer: Medial tilting and internal rotation of the distal fragment
questions.explanation: Cubitus varus ('gunstock deformity') following supracondylar fractures is caused by mechanical malunion of the distal fragment, specifically medial tilt, medial translation, and internal rotation. Contrary to historical belief, it is NOT due to asymmetric physeal growth arrest. The distal humeral physis contributes only 15-20% to humerus growth and does not correct the coronal plane malunion.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: In Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE), through which specific histological zone of the proximal femoral physis does mechanical displacement characteristically occur?
questions.explanation: In SCFE, the mechanical shearing separation occurs precisely through the zone of hypertrophy (specifically the cell hypertrophy and provisional calcification layers) of the growth plate. This zone has the lowest matrix-to-cell ratio and lacks structural collagen cross-linking, making it vulnerable to shear stresses during the adolescent growth spurt under hormonal influences.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 32-year-old man awakens after a deep sleep with his right upper arm draped over a hard chair. On examination, he has complete wrist drop and finger drop, loss of sensation over the first dorsal web space, but normal triceps strength and an intact triceps jerk. What is the diagnosis and site of compression?
options: Saturday night palsy; compression of radial nerve in the spiral groove
Crutch palsy; compression of radial nerve high in the axilla
Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome; entrapment at the Arcade of Frohse
Pronator teres syndrome; median nerve compression in the forearm
questions.answer: Saturday night palsy; compression of radial nerve in the spiral groove
questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy is a compression injury of the radial nerve in the spiral (radial) groove of the mid-shaft humerus. Because the motor branches to the triceps and anconeus arise proximal to the spiral groove (in the axilla), triceps power and elbow extension are fully preserved, but all wrist and finger extensors innervated distally (BR, ECRL, ECRB, EDC, ECU, EPL, etc.) are paralyzed, accompanied by numbness over the first dorsal web space.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: According to the nerve injury classifications of Seddon and Sunderland, which grade represents complete anatomical transection of the nerve trunk (axon, endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium)?
questions.explanation: Seddon's Neurotmesis corresponds to Sunderland Grade V: the nerve trunk is completely divided, with disruption of axons, endoneurial tubes, perineurium, and the external epineurium. Complete Wallerian degeneration occurs, and spontaneous recovery is impossible. Accurate surgical realignment and microscopic end-to-end neurorrhaphy (or nerve grafting) are obligatory.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old kitchen worker suffers a deep glass laceration on the volar wrist proximal to the flexor retinaculum. Examination reveals loss of finger abduction/adduction, a positive Froment's sign, and sensory loss over the hypothenar eminence and little finger. Which nerve is severed?
options: Ulnar nerve (low ulnar nerve injury at the wrist)
High radial nerve in the spiral groove
Median nerve at the pronator canal
Anterior interosseous nerve at the fibrous arch of FDS
questions.answer: Ulnar nerve (low ulnar nerve injury at the wrist)
questions.explanation: This presentation reflects low ulnar nerve palsy at the wrist: denervation of intrinsic hand muscles (interossei, medial two lumbricals, hypothenar muscles, and adductor pollicis). Loss of adductor pollicis causes a positive Froment's sign (patient flexes thumb IP joint via FPL, innervated by AIN, to hold paper). Sensation over the hypothenar area and little finger is lost.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What physiological phenomenon underlies Tinel's sign in a regenerating peripheral nerve, and at what approximate rate does axonal regeneration advance?
options: Percussion over unmyelinated axonal sprouts elicits paresthesias
Direct mechanical compression of hypertrophied Schwann cell myelin sheaths
Stimulation of retrograde axonal transport along intact collateral branches
Depolarization of motor endplate acetylcholine receptors along muscle fibers
questions.answer: Percussion over unmyelinated axonal sprouts elicits paresthesias
questions.explanation: Tinel's sign is elicited by gently tapping along the path of a damaged nerve from distal to proximal. When the percussion reaches the tips of regenerating, unmyelinated axonal sprouts (growth cones), tingling sensations (paresthesias) shoot into the cutaneous distribution of the nerve. A progressive distally advancing Tinel's sign indicates active axonal regeneration, which occurs at the rate of ~1 mm/day (or 1 mm per 24 hours, ~1 inch per month).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A patient sustains a high median nerve transection at the elbow. When asked to make a tight fist, the index and middle fingers remain extended while the ring and little fingers flex into the palm. What is this clinical posture termed?
questions.explanation: In high median nerve palsy, the patient cannot flex the thumb, index, or middle fingers when attempting to make a fist because of paralysis of the FPL, FDS, and the radial half of FDP (innervating digits 2 and 3). The ring and little fingers flex normally because the ulnar half of FDP is innervated by the intact ulnar nerve. This resulting posture resembles a priest giving a papal blessing ('Benediction sign' or 'pointing sign').
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What is the anatomical basis for the Ulnar Paradox in peripheral nerve injuries?
options: Clawing is more severe in low ulnar palsy than in high ulnar palsy
Clawing is more severe in high ulnar palsy than in low ulnar palsy
Sensory loss is completely absent in low ulnar nerve transections
Motor power of the adductor pollicis is fully preserved in low palsy
questions.answer: Clawing is more severe in low ulnar palsy than in high ulnar palsy
questions.explanation: The Ulnar Paradox states: 'the higher the lesion, the less severe the clawing.' In a low ulnar lesion (at the wrist), the intrinsic muscles (interossei, lumbricals 3 and 4) are paralyzed, but the extrinsic muscle Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) to digits 4 and 5 is intact; active FDP flexion unopposed by lumbricals produces severe clawing. In a high ulnar lesion (above elbow), FDP to digits 4 and 5 is also paralyzed, removing the primary flexor force at the IP joints, resulting in markedly less conspicuous clawing.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 25-year-old motorcyclist sustains a fracture of the neck of the fibula. On examination, he is unable to dorsiflex or evert his foot, walks with a steppage gait, and has numbness over the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is injured?
options: Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
Saphenous nerve at the adductor canal
Deep femoral nerve in the obturator groove
questions.explanation: The common peroneal nerve winds tightly around the neck of the fibula in a subcutaneous, vulnerable position where it can be crushed by direct blows or fibular neck fractures. Division causes loss of both deep peroneal (foot and toe dorsiflexors) and superficial peroneal (peroneus longus and brevis evertors) branches, causing classic foot drop, loss of eversion, equinovarus attitude during swing phase (steppage gait), and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: How does clinical examination reliably differentiate Pronator Teres Syndrome from Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?
options: Thenar sensation preserved in Carpal Tunnel, diminished in Pronator Teres
Phalen test is positive in Pronator Teres Syndrome, negative in Carpal Tunnel
Nocturnal paresthesias are exclusively present in Pronator Teres Syndrome
Motor weakness of the abductor pollicis brevis occurs only in Pronator Teres
questions.answer: Thenar sensation preserved in Carpal Tunnel, diminished in Pronator Teres
questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises approximately 5 to 6 cm proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum into the palm. Therefore, in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (compression inside the carpal tunnel under the retinaculum), sensation over the base of the thenar eminence is characteristically spared. In contrast, in proximal median nerve entrapment (Pronator Teres Syndrome), the palmar cutaneous branch is compressed, resulting in sensory loss over the thenar eminence.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A patient with an open infected midshaft humeral fracture sustains an irreparable 8-cm gap in the radial nerve. One year later, with all extensor muscles completely denervated, what is the classic tendon transfer of choice to restore wrist extension?
options: Transfer of Pronator Teres to Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
Transfer of Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) to Biceps brachii
Transfer of Brachioradialis to Flexor Digitorum Profundus
Transfer of Palmaris longus directly to Triceps tendon
questions.answer: Transfer of Pronator Teres to Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
questions.explanation: For permanent, irreparable radial nerve palsy, standard tendon transfer (the Robert Jones or modified transfer) restores function: 1. Pronator Teres (PT) transferred to Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB) to restore wrist extension; 2. Flexor Carpi Radialis (FCR) or Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) transferred to Extensor Digitorum Communis (EDC) to restore finger extension; 3. Palmaris Longus (PL) transferred to Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL) to restore thumb extension.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: In electrodiagnostic testing following acute peripheral nerve transection, how many days after injury do denervation changes (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) first appear on needle EMG?
questions.explanation: Following complete nerve division, distal axons conduct normally for up to 48-72 hours. Wallerian degeneration then begins and takes 2 to 3 weeks (14-21 days) to complete down the entire length of the distal nerve segment. Spontaneous denervation potentials (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) indicating loss of neural control over muscle membrane potentials appear on EMG only after Wallerian degeneration reaches the motor endplate, usually at 2-3 weeks.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child presents with knock-knees. On examination with medial femoral condyles in contact, the intermalleolar distance (IMD) measures 9 cm. Beyond what threshold is genu valgum considered pathological in a child older than 7 years?
options: Any degree of knee valgus at any age
questions.explanation: Physiological genu valgum is normal between ages 3 and 6 years, with spontaneous resolution expected by age 7 (normal adult valgus is 5-7 degrees). An intermalleolar distance (IMD) exceeding 8 cm in a child older than 7 years, or unilateral/progressive valgus, is considered pathological and requires workup (rickets, trauma, skeletal dysplasia) and possible surgical correction.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 10-year-old child with post-traumatic cubitus varus following a malunited supracondylar fracture is scheduled for corrective osteotomy. Which procedure is the classic standard technique described by French?
options: Lateral closing-wedge osteotomy of the distal humerus
Medial opening-wedge distraction osteotomy with fibular graft
Dome-shaped derotation osteotomy of the radial neck
Resection of the lateral epicondyle with annular ligament release
questions.answer: Lateral closing-wedge osteotomy of the distal humerus
questions.explanation: The classic French osteotomy for cubitus varus is a lateral closing-wedge osteotomy of the supracondylar distal humerus. The medial cortical hinge is preserved, a predetermined triangular wedge of bone is excised from the lateral cortex, the osteotomy is closed to restore the carrying angle, and stability is maintained using crossed screws or K-wires.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What is the primary mechanical advantage of an opening-wedge osteotomy compared to a closing-wedge osteotomy?
options: Opening-wedge preserves bone length, closing-wedge causes shortening
Opening-wedge allows immediate full weightbearing without internal fixation
Opening-wedge completely eliminates the requirement for any bone grafting
Opening-wedge carries zero risk of neurovascular stretching or tension injury
questions.answer: Opening-wedge preserves bone length, closing-wedge causes shortening
questions.explanation: An opening-wedge osteotomy corrects angular deformity while increasing overall bone length (beneficial when the injured limb is already short), but creates a structural gap requiring autologous/allograft bone grafting and rigid plate fixation. In contrast, a closing-wedge osteotomy achieves direct bone-on-bone contact with faster union, but inherently shortens the limb.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What fundamental clinical feature distinguishes a structural deformity from a postural (functional) deformity?
options: Structural deformity is fixed, postural is passively fully correctable
Structural deformity involves joints only, postural involves long bones only
Structural deformity occurs exclusively in adults, postural occurs in children
Structural deformity spontaneously corrects, postural requires major surgery
questions.answer: Structural deformity is fixed, postural is passively fully correctable
questions.explanation: A postural (functional or dynamic) deformity is caused by habitual posture or muscle imbalance; there are no permanent contractures, and the deformity can be actively or passively corrected completely to neutral. A structural (fixed) deformity is associated with permanent morphological changes in bones, joints, ligaments, or contracted capsules, and cannot be corrected to neutral by passive manipulation.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 12-year-old boy with severe idiopathic genu valgum of 18 degrees has open physes. What minimally invasive guided growth procedure is indicated to correct this deformity without performing an osteotomy?
options: Temporary medial hemiepiphysiodesis using extra-periosteal tension-band plates
Complete bilateral open epiphyseodesis of both femoral and tibial physes
High tibial closing-wedge osteotomy with a T-plate
Immediate Ilizarov ring frame application with acute 20-degree valgus correction
questions.answer: Temporary medial hemiepiphysiodesis using extra-periosteal tension-band plates
questions.explanation: Temporary hemiepiphysiodesis (guided growth) using extra-periosteal non-locking tension-band plates ('8-plates' and cannulated screws) straddling the medial aspect of the physis inhibits growth on the medial side while allowing continued growth on the lateral side. As the child grows, the valgus deformity progressively straightens. Once corrected, the implant is removed, allowing normal symmetrical physeal growth.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.topicTitle: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.prompt: A 56-year-old patient with long-standing diabetic neuropathy presents with a painless, swollen, completely destroyed, and flail Charcot ankle joint. Which operative procedure is indicated to provide a stable, painless, weight-bearing extremity?
options: Continuous passive motion and early weight-bearing
questions.explanation: Charcot neuroarthropathy results in progressive joint destruction, ligamentous laxity, fragmentation, and instability due to loss of protective pain and proprioceptive sensation. Total joint replacement is contraindicated because lack of proprioception causes catastrophic early loosening. Arthrodesis (joint fusion) using rigid internal/external fixation is the surgical procedure of choice to establish a stable, plantigrade, non-ulcerating foot.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.topicTitle: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.prompt: What is the optimal functional position for arthrodesis (fusion) of the hip joint in an adult manual laborer?
options: 20 to 25 degrees of flexion, 0 to 5 degrees of abduction, and neutral rotation
45 degrees of flexion, 15 degrees of adduction, and 15 degrees of internal rotation
Complete neutral extension (0 degrees), 20 degrees of external rotation, and 10 degrees of adduction
90 degrees of flexion and 30 degrees of abduction to allow comfortable sitting
questions.answer: 20 to 25 degrees of flexion, 0 to 5 degrees of abduction, and neutral rotation
questions.explanation: The ideal position for arthrodesis of the hip joint is 20 to 25 degrees of flexion, neutral to 5 degrees of abduction (prevents pelvic tilt), and neutral rotation. This allows the patient to walk with an acceptable gait without excessive lordosis, sit comfortably without excessive pelvic tilt, and stand upright with minimum compensatory spinal strain.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.topicTitle: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.prompt: What is the optimal functional position for arthrodesis of the adult wrist joint to preserve maximal grasp power?
options: 20 to 25 degrees of dorsiflexion (extension) with 5 degrees of ulnar deviation
30 degrees of palmar flexion with 15 degrees of radial deviation
Complete neutral position (0 degrees flexion/extension) with maximal pronation
45 degrees of dorsiflexion with 20 degrees of radial deviation
questions.answer: 20 to 25 degrees of dorsiflexion (extension) with 5 degrees of ulnar deviation
questions.explanation: The optimal position for wrist arthrodesis is 20 to 25 degrees of dorsiflexion (extension) and slight ulnar deviation (5 degrees). This position mimics the natural posture of the wrist during powerful power-grip activities, optimizing length-tension relationships for the long digital flexor tendons.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.topicTitle: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.prompt: What is the surgical definition of an excision arthroplasty (such as the Girdlestone procedure for the hip joint)?
options: Resection of bone ends forming a mobile pseudoarthrosis
Rigid joint arthrodesis using crossed cancellous lag screws
Prosthetic joint replacement with metal and polyethylene
Interposition of synthetic silicone caps over cartilage
questions.answer: Resection of bone ends forming a mobile pseudoarthrosis
questions.explanation: Excision arthroplasty involves complete surgical removal of the articulating bone ends (e.g., Girdlestone resection arthroplasty of the hip involves excision of the femoral head and neck). The resulting dead space fills with fibrous scar tissue, creating a mobile pseudoarthrosis that eliminates pain (e.g., in refractory septic arthritis or failed total hip replacement) at the expense of limb shortening and instability.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.topicTitle: Treatment of Orthopaedic Disorders: A General Review
questions.prompt: Following arthroscopic lysis of knee adhesions or ACL reconstruction, what is the primary biological benefit of a Continuous Passive Motion (CPM) machine?
options: Prevents adhesions and enhances synovial cartilage nutrition
Provides rigid axial compression to promote direct primary bone union
Immobilizes the joint to permit undisturbed ligamentous remodeling
Eliminates the requirement for systemic postoperative thromboprophylaxis
questions.answer: Prevents adhesions and enhances synovial cartilage nutrition
questions.explanation: Continuous Passive Motion (CPM), introduced by Robert Salter, moves the joint passively through a controlled range of motion without active muscle contraction. This continuous movement promotes synovial fluid circulation, provides metabolic nutrition to healing articular cartilage, minimizes intra-articular adhesion and scar formation, and accelerates clearance of hemarthrosis and periarticular edema.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old rugby player falls onto his abducted, externally rotated right arm. On examination, the normal rounded contour of the right deltoid is flattened, the acromion is prominent with a subacromial hollow, the elbow is held in slight abduction, and the patient cannot touch his opposite shoulder with the affected hand (positive Dugas test). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is the classic presentation of an acute anterior dislocation of the shoulder (most commonly subcoracoid): flattening of the deltoid, prominent acromion, subacromial hollow, arm held in slight abduction and external rotation, and inability to adduct the arm to bring the hand to the opposite shoulder (Dugas test / Hamilton's ruler sign / Callaway's test).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: What is the precise step-by-step sequence of maneuvers described by Kocher for closed reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation?
options: Traction -> External rotation -> Adduction -> Internal rotation
Adduction -> Internal rotation -> Direct pressure -> Traction
Hyperabduction -> Elevation -> Downward traction -> Neutral rotation
questions.answer: Traction -> External rotation -> Adduction -> Internal rotation
questions.explanation: Kocher's method consists of 4 distinct steps: 1. Traction in the line of the humerus with elbow flexed at 90 degrees; 2. External rotation of the arm slowly until resistance is felt (relaxes subscapularis and levers head out); 3. Adduction of the elbow across the front of the chest to the midline; 4. Internal rotation of the arm bringing the hand to the opposite shoulder (slides humeral head into glenoid fossa).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: On an anteroposterior radiograph with internal rotation of the shoulder following recurrent anterior dislocations, a wedge-shaped compression fracture is visible on the posterolateral aspect of the humeral head. What is this lesion termed?
questions.explanation: A Hill-Sachs lesion is a compression/impact depression fracture on the posterolateral aspect of the humeral head. It is produced when the dislocated humeral head impacts against the hard, anterior-inferior rim of the glenoid. In contrast, a Bankart lesion affects the anterior-inferior glenoid labrum/rim.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure with severe shoulder pain. The arm is locked in adduction and internal rotation, with complete loss of external rotation. AP radiograph shows a symmetrical, rounded humeral head resembling a 'light bulb'. What is the diagnosis?
options: Posterior dislocation of the shoulder joint
Fracture of the greater tuberosity with subacromial impingement
questions.answer: Posterior dislocation of the shoulder joint
questions.explanation: Posterior shoulder dislocation is notoriously missed (in up to 50% of cases) and classically occurs after epileptic seizures, electric shocks, or electroconvulsive therapy due to violent contraction of the internal rotators (latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, subscapularis) overpowering external rotators. Hallmark signs: arm locked in internal rotation and adduction; AP radiograph shows 'light-bulb sign'.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: In Neer's classification of proximal humeral fractures, what criteria must a bone fragment meet to be classified as a displaced 'part'?
options: Displacement greater than 1.0 cm or angulation greater than 45 degrees
Displacement greater than 2.0 cm or angulation greater than 90 degrees
Any visible fracture line regardless of displacement
Displacement greater than 5 mm with associated neurovascular deficit
questions.answer: Displacement greater than 1.0 cm or angulation greater than 45 degrees
questions.explanation: Neer's classification is based on displacement of 4 anatomical segments: 1. Greater tuberosity; 2. Lesser tuberosity; 3. Humeral head (articular segment); 4. Humeral shaft. A fragment is considered a 'part' ONLY if it is displaced more than 1 cm (10 mm) or angulated more than 45 degrees from its anatomical position. An undisplaced fracture is a 'one-part' fracture even if all 4 lines are present.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female sustains a distal third spiral fracture of the humerus (Holstein-Lewis fracture). On examination, she has wrist drop and sensory loss over the first dorsal web space. Which structure is at high risk of entrapment between fracture fragments?
questions.explanation: The Holstein-Lewis fracture is a spiral fracture of the distal third of the humeral shaft. At this level, the radial nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to pass from the posterior to the anterior compartment, tethering it firmly to the bone. Distal third spiral fractures have a high incidence of radial nerve entrapment or laceration (up to 20-25%).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male with a closed midshaft transverse humeral fracture presents with complete primary radial nerve palsy. What is the consensus first-line management strategy?
options: Closed reduction and splinting with observation for 3 to 4 months
Emergency open surgical exploration of the radial nerve within 6 hours
Immediate resection of the fractured humerus with primary sural nerve grafting
Emergency posterior arm compartment fasciotomy with immediate tendon transfers
questions.answer: Closed reduction and splinting with observation for 3 to 4 months
questions.explanation: Primary radial nerve palsy accompanying a closed humeral shaft fracture is almost always a neuropraxia or axonotmesis in continuity (>90% recover spontaneously within 3-4 months). Therefore, initial management is closed fracture reduction and splinting (U-slab/functional brace) and watchful waiting with serial clinical and EMG examinations. Exploration is reserved for open fractures, secondary palsy developing after manipulation, or failure of recovery after 3-4 months.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: In a fracture of the middle third of the clavicle, what characteristic displacement forces are exerted by attached muscle groups on the proximal and distal fragments?
options: Proximal fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid, distal down by arm weight
Proximal fragment pulled down by subclavius, distal pulled up by trapezius
Both fragments displaced posteriorly by the powerful pectoralis minor
Fragments displaced anteriorly by intercostal muscles with intact skin bridge
questions.answer: Proximal fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid, distal down by arm weight
questions.explanation: In middle-third clavicular fractures, the sternocleidomastoid muscle pulls the medial (proximal) fragment superiorly and posteriorly. The lateral (distal) fragment is displaced inferiorly, anteriorly, and medially by the gravitational weight of the unsupported upper extremity and the strong adductor pull of the pectoralis major muscle.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: In an active young adult, what threshold of superior displacement of a greater tuberosity fracture of the humerus mandates open reduction and internal fixation to prevent subacromial impingement?
options: Displacement greater than 5 mm, or over 3 mm in athletes
Displacement greater than 15 mm in all patient populations
Any degree of displacement greater than 1 mm regardless of activity
Displacement greater than 10 mm measured on axial views alone
questions.answer: Displacement greater than 5 mm, or over 3 mm in athletes
questions.explanation: The greater tuberosity serves as the insertion site for the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor tendons. Superior displacement of > 5 mm (or > 3 mm in high-demand overhead athletes) causes mechanical blockage and painful subacromial impingement against the acromion and coracoacromial arch during abduction, warranting surgical anatomical reduction and screw or suture-anchor fixation.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.topicTitle: Injuries Around the Shoulder, Fracture Humerus
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation. Clinical examination reveals deltoid weakness and sensory numbness over the lateral aspect of the upper arm ('regimental badge' area). Which nerve is injured?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus immediately inferior to the glenohumeral joint capsule. During anterior shoulder dislocation, the displaced humeral head stretches the nerve, causing neuropraxia in 10-15% of cases. Hallmark signs are paralysis/weakness of the deltoid muscle and sensory loss over the upper lateral aspect of the arm ('regimental badge' area).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 7-year-old boy falls onto his outstretched hand with the elbow hyperextended. Examination shows a swollen, deformed elbow with S-shaped anterior skin puckering. Radiographs show distal humeral metaphysis disruption with posterior and superior displacement of the distal fragment. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Extension-type supracondylar fractures account for >95% of supracondylar fractures in children, classically caused by a fall onto an outstretched hand with hyperextended elbow. The distal fragment is displaced posteriorly and tilted into extension, while the sharp spike of the proximal fragment juts anteriorly into the brachialis muscle. Gartland Type III is completely displaced with disrupted cortices.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: What crucial anatomical landmark relationship distinguishes a supracondylar fracture of the humerus from a posterior dislocation of the elbow joint?
options: Three-point triangle preserved in supracondylar, disrupted in dislocation
Three-point triangle disrupted in supracondylar, preserved in dislocation
Radial head alignment with capitellum disrupted in supracondylar fracture
Carrying angle remains unchanged in dislocation but reversed in supracondylar
questions.answer: Three-point triangle preserved in supracondylar, disrupted in dislocation
questions.explanation: The 'three-point bony relationship' consists of the tip of the olecranon and the two epicondyles: in 90 degrees of flexion they form an equilateral triangle; in full extension they lie in a straight horizontal line. In supracondylar fracture, the fracture line is entirely above the condyles, so the relationship among the epicondyles and olecranon remains normal. In elbow dislocation, the olecranon is displaced relative to the epicondyles, disrupting the triangle.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: In a Gartland Type III supracondylar fracture of the humerus with posteromedial displacement of the distal fragment, which neurovascular structure is at greatest risk of injury from the proximal bone spike?
questions.explanation: The direction of distal fragment displacement dictates which neurovascular structures are endangered: When the distal fragment is displaced posteromedially, the sharp proximal fragment juts anterolaterally, endangering the radial nerve. Conversely, when the distal fragment is displaced posterolaterally, the proximal spike juts anteromedially, endangering the brachial artery and median nerve.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child in an above-elbow slab for a supracondylar fracture develops severe forearm pain. The fingers are held in slight flexion. Attempting to passively extend the fingers produces excruciating volar forearm pain. What is the earliest pathognomonic sign of impending Volkmann's ischemia?
options: Severe pain on gentle passive finger extension
Complete absence of palpable radial arterial pulse
Profound pallor and coldness of all five fingertips
Complete sensory anesthesia in median nerve distribution
questions.answer: Severe pain on gentle passive finger extension
questions.explanation: Severe pain out of proportion to the injury, markedly exacerbated by passive extension of the fingers, is the earliest and most sensitive sign of impending Volkmann's ischemia (forearm compartment syndrome). The presence of a radial pulse does NOT exclude ischemia because capillary perfusion pressure is overwhelmed long before major arterial pulses cease. Pallor, pulselessness, and paralysis are late, irreversible signs.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: Why is a displaced fracture of the lateral condyle of the humerus in a 6-year-old child termed a 'fracture of necessity' requiring anatomical open reduction and internal fixation?
options: Intra-articular physeal fracture prone to non-union and cubitus valgus
Extra-articular metaphyseal fracture that spontaneously realigns cleanly
Prone to immediate acute median nerve transection and Volkmann ischemic contracture
Exclusively associated with recurrent posterior subluxation of the radial head
questions.answer: Intra-articular physeal fracture prone to non-union and cubitus valgus
questions.explanation: Lateral condyle fracture is a Salter-Harris Type IV intra-articular physeal fracture through the capitulum and trochlear groove. Because the extensor muscles attach to it, the fragment is rotated and tilted. Synovial fluid inhibits healing. Failure to achieve anatomical reduction leads to non-union, growth arrest, progressive cubitus valgus deformity, and tardy ulnar nerve palsy 10-20 years later. Hence, it is a 'fracture of necessity'.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 3-year-old toddler is swung by the wrists by an adult. The child cries and refuses to use the arm, holding the elbow in slight flexion and pronation. Radiographs are normal. What is the diagnosis and reduction maneuver?
options: Pulled elbow, reduced by supination with radial head pressure, then flexion
Radial head dislocation, reduced by continuous forearm pronation and extension
Nursemaid elbow, treated with immediate open reduction and annular ligament suture
Elbow subluxation, reduced by longitudinal hyperextension and valgus distraction
questions.answer: Pulled elbow, reduced by supination with radial head pressure, then flexion
questions.explanation: Pulled elbow occurs in children under 5 years when sudden longitudinal traction is applied to an extended, pronated arm. The immature, loose annular ligament slips over the rounded head of the radius into the radiocapitellar joint, where it becomes entrapped. Closed reduction is performed by supporting the elbow with thumb over radial head, rapidly supinating the forearm, and then fully flexing the elbow. A subtle 'click' is felt, and the child immediately resumes using the arm.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: An adult falls onto an outstretched hand and sustains a Mason Type II radial head fracture (>30% articular surface, displaced >2 mm) without mechanical block. What is the treatment of choice?
options: Open reduction and internal fixation with low-profile countersunk mini-screws
Radial head excision with prolonged immobilization in a sling
Simple sling immobilization for 8 weeks without surgery
questions.answer: Open reduction and internal fixation with low-profile countersunk mini-screws
questions.explanation: According to the Mason classification of radial head fractures: Type I is undisplaced (conservative); Type II is a displaced partial articular fracture (>2 mm displacement, >30% articular surface); Type III is a severely comminuted fracture involving the entire radial head. For Mason Type II, ORIF with low-profile headless screws restoring articular congruity is the procedure of choice. Radial head excision in a young adult is avoided to prevent proximal radial migration.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: Why is a displaced olecranon fracture treated with tension band wiring (TBW) rather than conservative casting?
options: Converts triceps tensile distraction into articular compressive forces
Provides rigid locked fixed-angle neutralization of all rotational torques
Eliminates triceps extensor power to allow passive ligamentous healing
Acts as a flexible intramedullary splint preserving microvascular supply
questions.answer: Converts triceps tensile distraction into articular compressive forces
questions.explanation: The olecranon forms the trochlear notch of the elbow joint. When fractured, the triceps muscle continually pulls the proximal fragment proximally, causing displacement and articular incongruity. A tension band construct (two parallel K-wires and a figure-of-eight stainless steel wire loop) harnesses the tensile pull of the triceps during elbow flexion and converts it into compressive force across the articular fracture surface, allowing early active movement.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old male sustains a severely displaced, comminuted intercondylar T- or Y-shaped distal humerus fracture. What is the gold-standard surgical approach and fixation construct?
options: Olecranon osteotomy with condylar reduction and bicolumnar plating
Anterior Henry approach with single lateral dynamic compression plate
Minimally invasive percutaneous pinning under fluoroscopy without exposure
Primary total elbow arthroplasty as the mandatory first-line intervention
questions.answer: Olecranon osteotomy with condylar reduction and bicolumnar plating
questions.explanation: Intercondylar T- or Y-shaped fractures of the distal humerus involve complete intra-articular and metaphyseal dissociation. Surgical restoration requires direct exposure of the articular surface via a chevron olecranon osteotomy (or triceps-sparing approach), anatomical reduction and screw fixation of the articular condyles, and rigid stabilization of both medial and lateral columns using dual locking plates in a 90-90 (orthogonal) or parallel configuration.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.prompt: Tardy ulnar nerve palsy is a classic late sequela developing 10 to 20 years following which pediatric elbow fracture?
options: Lateral condyle malunion or nonunion causing cubitus valgus
Medial epicondyle avulsion nonunion causing severe cubitus varus
Supracondylar fracture malunion producing classic gunstock deformity
Olecranon nonunion causing chronic posterior subluxation of the ulna
questions.answer: Lateral condyle malunion or nonunion causing cubitus valgus
questions.explanation: Tardy ulnar nerve palsy develops decades after an ununited or malunited fracture of the lateral condyle of the humerus. The arrest of lateral column growth combined with continued medial growth produces a progressive cubitus valgus deformity. With increasing valgus, the ulnar nerve is stretched around the medial epicondyle, leading to chronic friction neuritis, numbness in digits 4 and 5, and clawing. Treatment is anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old male sustains an isolated fracture of the proximal third of the ulna associated with anterior dislocation of the radial head. What eponymic fracture-dislocation is this?
questions.explanation: A Monteggia fracture-dislocation is a fracture of the shaft of the ulna associated with dislocation of the radio-capitellar joint (radial head). In Bado Type I (most common, ~60-70%), the ulnar fracture is angulated anteriorly, and the radial head is dislocated anteriorly. Bado Type II involves posterior dislocation; Type III involves lateral dislocation; Type IV involves fractures of both radius and ulna with radial head dislocation.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: In a Monteggia fracture-dislocation, which peripheral nerve is at highest risk of stretch or entrapment by the dislocated radial head?
questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), the deep motor branch of the radial nerve, passes through the supinator muscle (Arcade of Frohse) immediately adjacent to the neck of the radius. When the radial head dislocates anteriorly or anterolaterally in a Monteggia fracture, the PIN is stretched across the dislocated radial head, resulting in PIN palsy (loss of MCP finger extension and thumb extension with preserved wrist extension due to ECRL innervation).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old motorcyclist falls onto a pronated forearm and sustains a fracture of the distal third radius shaft accompanied by disruption and dislocation of the Distal Radioulnar Joint (DRUJ). What is this injury termed?
questions.explanation: A Galeazzi fracture-dislocation consists of a fracture of the distal third of the radius shaft with disruption/dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) and tearing of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC). It is also known as a 'fracture of necessity' because closed casting almost always fails due to the deforming forces of the pronator quadratus and brachioradialis; it requires rigid open reduction and plate fixation of the radius.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman sustains a Colles' fracture following a fall on an outstretched hand. What are the classical displacement components of the distal fragment?
options: Dorsal displacement, dorsal tilt, radial displacement, radial tilt, supination, and impaction
Volar displacement, volar tilt, ulnar displacement, ulnar tilt, pronation, and distraction
Dorsal displacement, volar tilt, radial displacement, pronation, distraction, and internal rotation
Volar displacement, dorsal tilt, ulnar displacement, supination, impaction, and lengthening
questions.answer: Dorsal displacement, dorsal tilt, radial displacement, radial tilt, supination, and impaction
questions.explanation: In Colles' fracture (extra-articular fracture of the distal radius within 2.5 cm of the articular surface), the distal fragment undergoes 6 classical displacements: 1. Dorsal displacement (shifts backward); 2. Dorsal tilt (articular surface tilts dorsally); 3. Radial displacement (shifts outward); 4. Radial tilt (articular surface tilts radially); 5. Supination (rotates backward relative to proximal shaft); 6. Impaction (telescoping causing loss of radial length/radial height).
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: On standard radiographs of a normal adult wrist, what are the normal reference parameters for radial inclination and palmar (volar) tilt of the distal radius articular surface?
options: Radial inclination 21 to 23 degrees, palmar tilt 11 to 12 degrees
Radial inclination 11 to 12 degrees, palmar tilt 21 to 23 degrees
Radial inclination 30 to 35 degrees, dorsal tilt 10 to 15 degrees
Radial inclination 5 to 10 degrees, neutral tilt 0 degrees
questions.answer: Radial inclination 21 to 23 degrees, palmar tilt 11 to 12 degrees
questions.explanation: On a standard posteroanterior (PA) radiograph, the distal radius articular surface angles towards the ulna with a normal radial inclination of 21 to 23 degrees (and a radial height of 11-12 mm). On a true lateral radiograph, the articular surface tilts forward with a normal palmar (volar) tilt of 11 to 12 degrees. In Colles' fracture, radial inclination is reduced and volar tilt is reversed into a dorsal tilt.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old male falls onto the back of his flexed wrist, presenting with a 'garden-spade' deformity. Radiographs show a distal radius metaphyseal fracture with volar displacement and volar tilt of the distal fragment. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Smith's fracture (reverse Colles' fracture) is caused by a fall onto a flexed wrist or a direct blow to the dorsum of the flexed wrist. The fracture line is extra-articular at the distal radius metaphysis, and the distal fragment is displaced anteriorly (volarly) and tilted volarly, producing the classic 'garden-spade' deformity. It is inherently unstable and usually requires buttress plate fixation.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: How does a Barton's fracture anatomically differ from both Colles' and Smith's fractures?
options: Extra-articular metaphyseal fracture with dorsal comminution
Extra-articular metaphyseal fracture with volar displacement
Isolated avulsion fracture of the radial styloid process
questions.explanation: While Colles' and Smith's fractures are extra-articular metaphyseal fractures, Barton's fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation or subluxation of the radiocarpal joint. An oblique fracture line shears off either the dorsal lip (Dorsal Barton's) or the volar lip (Volar Barton's) of the distal radius articular surface, and the entire carpus displaces along with the articular bone fragment. Volar Barton's is treated with a volar buttress plate.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male presents with anatomical snuffbox tenderness and pain on axial loading of the thumb following a fall on an outstretched hand. Initial plain radiographs of the wrist are normal. What is the mandatory management protocol?
options: Scaphoid cast and repeat radiographs in 10 to 14 days, or early MRI
Reassurance with an elastic crepe bandage and immediate normal return to sports
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation with a headless cannulated screw
Short-arm volar slab for 48 hours followed by vigorous active wrist mobilization
questions.answer: Scaphoid cast and repeat radiographs in 10 to 14 days, or early MRI
questions.explanation: A high index of suspicion for scaphoid fracture must be maintained whenever anatomical snuffbox tenderness is present following a fall on an outstretched hand. Undisplaced hairline fractures of the scaphoid waist are notoriously invisible on initial radiographs (false negative in up to 15-20%). The standard protocol mandates applying a scaphoid plaster cast and repeating radiographs after 10-14 days (when bone resorption along the fracture line makes it visible), or performing an early MRI/CT scan.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: Why is a fracture traversing the proximal pole of the scaphoid at high risk of developing avascular necrosis (AVN)?
options: Retrograde blood supply enters distally, leaving proximal pole ischemic
Antegrade arterial supply from dorsal carpal arch enters proximal pole directly
Scaphoid is completely surrounded by thick avascular fibrous periosteum
High mechanical tensile strain stimulates osteoclast resorption of proximal bone
questions.answer: Retrograde blood supply enters distally, leaving proximal pole ischemic
questions.explanation: The arterial blood supply to the scaphoid is retrograde: branches of the radial artery enter the bone through vascular foramina on the non-articular dorsal ridge and distal tubercle, flowing proximally within the bone to supply the waist and proximal pole. A fracture through the waist or proximal pole severs this intraosseous arterial network, rendering the proximal fragment completely ischemic and predisposing it to avascular necrosis (AVN) in nearly 100% of proximal pole fractures.
questions.subject: Orthopedics

questions.topic: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.topicTitle: Injuries of the Forearm and Wrist
questions.prompt: On a true lateral radiograph of the wrist following high-energy trauma, the lunate maintains its normal articulation with the distal radius, but the capitate is dislocated dorsally out of the lunate cup. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In perilunate dislocation, the lunate remains in its normal anatomical position within the lunate fossa of the distal radius, but the rest of the carpus (headed by the capitate) is displaced dorsally.
